question: (a) Define research and nursing research, and list the characteristics of good research. (4 marks) (b) Explain the steps of the quantitative research process, with a flow diagram. (8 marks) (c) Explain the need and importance of research in nursing. (3 marks)

answer_html:
(a) Definitions and characteristics of good research (4 marks)

Definitions

  • Research is a systematic inquiry that uses disciplined (scientific) methods to answer questions or solve problems, with the aim of developing or refining knowledge.
  • Nursing research is systematic inquiry designed to develop trustworthy evidence about issues important to the nursing profession – nursing practice, education, administration and informatics (Polit and Beck). Its ultimate aim is better care and outcomes for patients, families and communities.

Characteristics of good research

  • Systematic and logical – follows an orderly, planned sequence of steps.
  • Empirical – based on observable, measurable evidence gathered from reality, not on opinion.
  • Objective and unbiased – findings are not influenced by the researcher's personal feelings.
  • Controlled – the influence of extraneous factors is reduced as far as possible.
  • Valid and reliable – uses accurate tools and sound methods so that results can be trusted.
  • Replicable – described clearly enough to be repeated by others.
  • Generalisable – findings can be applied beyond the sample, within limits.
  • Ethical – protects the rights, dignity and safety of participants.
  • Clearly defined purpose, adequate analysis, honest reporting of limitations, and conclusions justified by the data.

(b) Steps of the quantitative research process (8 marks)

The research process is a series of logical, interrelated steps that the researcher follows from identifying a problem to using the findings. It is commonly described in five phases.

Phase 1 – Conceptual (thinking) phase

  1. Formulating and delimiting the research problem – identifying a researchable problem from practice, literature or theory, and narrowing it into a clear statement and research questions or objectives.
  2. Reviewing the related literature – to learn what is already known, find gaps, refine the problem and choose methods and tools.
  3. Clinical fieldwork – spending time in the clinical setting to understand the practical realities.
  4. Developing a conceptual or theoretical framework and conceptual/operational definitions of key terms.
  5. Formulating hypotheses – predictions of the expected relationship between variables (in experimental and correlational studies).

Phase 2 – Design and planning phase

  1. Selecting the research approach and design – quantitative approach; experimental, quasi-experimental or non-experimental design.
  2. Developing the intervention protocol (in intervention studies) – for example a structured teaching programme.
  3. Identifying the population and the setting.
  4. Designing the sampling plan – sampling technique, sample size, inclusion and exclusion criteria.
  5. Selecting or developing tools to measure the variables – questionnaire, observation checklist, rating scale, physiological measures – and establishing their validity and reliability.
  6. Planning ethical protection – approval of the institutional ethics committee, permission from authorities, informed consent, confidentiality.
  7. Finalising the plan and conducting a pilot study – a small-scale trial to test the feasibility of the study and the tool.

Phase 3 – Empirical phase

  1. Collecting the data according to the plan, within the stipulated time.
  2. Preparing the data for analysis – editing, coding and entering the data into a master sheet or computer.

Phase 4 – Analytic phase

  1. Analysing the data – descriptive statistics (frequency, percentage, mean, SD) and inferential statistics (t-test, chi-square, correlation) to answer the questions and test hypotheses.
  2. Interpreting the results – explaining the meaning of the findings, comparing them with other studies and stating limitations.

Phase 5 – Dissemination phase

  1. Communicating the findings – writing the research report or thesis, presenting at conferences, publishing in journals.
  2. Utilising the findings in nursing practice, education and administration – which often raises new problems for further research.

The process is cyclical – the end of one study is often the beginning of the next.

(c) Need and importance of research in nursing (3 marks)

  • Builds a scientific body of nursing knowledge and supports evidence-based practice instead of tradition and routine.
  • Improves the quality and safety of patient care and patient outcomes; tests new nursing interventions (for example KMC, pressure-injury prevention, pain management).
  • Promotes cost-effective care and efficient use of resources.
  • Strengthens nursing education (teaching methods, curriculum, simulation) and nursing administration (staffing, job satisfaction, retention).
  • Enhances professional status, autonomy and accountability – a profession must generate its own knowledge.
  • Guides health policy and national programmes with nursing evidence.
  • Develops critical thinking and problem-solving in nurses.

(d) Research process in qualitative studies – how it differs

Point Quantitative process Qualitative process
Sequence Fixed, linear sequence of steps decided in advance Flexible and emergent; steps overlap and are revised during the study
Literature review Done fully before data collection Often limited at first to avoid preconceptions
Hypotheses Usually stated and tested Not stated; questions are open and exploratory
Sampling Large, preferably random samples Small, purposive samples until data saturation
Data collection and analysis Separate, sequential steps Collection and analysis go on together
Data Numbers analysed statistically Words and observations analysed for themes

(e) Application of the research process – an example

  • Problem – "Effectiveness of a structured teaching programme (STP) on knowledge regarding kangaroo mother care among postnatal mothers of low birth weight babies in selected hospitals."
  • Literature review – studies on KMC knowledge and on the effect of teaching programmes; a framework such as the general system theory (input – teaching, throughput – learning, output – knowledge gain).
  • Hypothesis – the mean post-test knowledge score will be significantly higher than the pre-test score.
  • Design – one-group pre-test post-test (pre-experimental) design; population – postnatal mothers of LBW babies; sample – 60 mothers selected by purposive sampling, with inclusion and exclusion criteria.
  • Tool – a structured knowledge questionnaire, its content validity checked by experts and reliability by the split-half or test–retest method; pilot study on about 10% of the sample.
  • Ethics – approval of the institutional ethics committee, permission of the hospital, written informed consent.
  • Data collection – pre-test, STP, post-test after 7 days; analysis – frequency, percentage, mean, SD, paired t-test and chi-square; interpretation and discussion with earlier studies.
  • Dissemination and utilisation – report, conference presentation, and use of the STP in the postnatal ward.

(f) Common terms used in the research process

  • Concept / construct – an abstract idea (pain, anxiety, coping) that must be defined and measured.
  • Population – the entire group of people with the characteristics of interest; sample – the subset actually studied.
  • Data – the information collected; tool (instrument) – the device used to collect it (questionnaire, scale, checklist).
  • Assumption – a statement accepted as true without proof (for example, "mothers will answer honestly").
  • Delimitation – the boundaries set by the researcher (setting, sample, period); limitation – a weakness beyond the researcher's control that restricts generalisation.

Nursing importance

  • Every nurse is at least a consumer of research; knowing the research process allows her to read studies critically, take part in data collection safely and ethically, and apply sound findings at the bedside.

Conclusion Research is a systematic, ethical and logical method of answering questions. Following the steps of the research process – from problem identification to utilisation – produces trustworthy evidence that improves nursing practice, education and administration.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: (a) Classify research according to different criteria. (5 marks) (b) Explain the role of the nurse in research. (5 marks) (c) Describe the research priority areas in nursing in India. (5 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Classification of research (5 marks)

Basis Types Meaning / example
Purpose (use of findings) Basic (pure) To develop or refine theory and knowledge, without immediate application (for example, testing a theory of self-care)
Applied To solve practical problems (for example, effect of warm compresses on IV infiltration)
Action research Practitioners study and solve a problem in their own setting while bringing change (for example, improving hand-hygiene compliance in a ward)
Approach Quantitative Numerical data, objective measurement, statistical analysis
Qualitative Narrative data, understanding experiences and meanings (phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography)
Mixed methods Combines both
Design / control Experimental (true, quasi, pre-experimental) Researcher manipulates the independent variable
Non-experimental No manipulation – descriptive, correlational, survey, comparative
Objective Descriptive, exploratory, explanatory, predictive, evaluative Describes phenomena, explores new areas, explains relationships, predicts outcomes, evaluates programmes
Time dimension Cross-sectional (data at one point of time), longitudinal (same subjects over time); retrospective (looks back), prospective (follows forward)
Setting Laboratory (controlled) and field (naturalistic) research
Others Historical, philosophical, methodological (tool development), epidemiological, operational research

(b) Role of the nurse in research (5 marks)

1. According to educational preparation (as commonly expected)

  • Diploma and B.Sc. nurses – consumers of research: identify clinical problems, read and critique studies at a basic level, assist in data collection, apply evidence in practice, and protect patients taking part in studies.
  • M.Sc. nurses – conduct and supervise studies, collaborate with other researchers, guide students, evaluate and introduce evidence into practice.
  • Doctoral (PhD) nurses – independent investigators, develop theories and research programmes, obtain grants, mentor other researchers, and influence policy.

2. Specific roles

  • Problem identifier – recognises gaps and problems in daily practice.
  • Principal or co-investigator – plans and conducts studies.
  • Data collector – gathers data accurately, ethically and without bias.
  • Patient advocate – ensures informed consent, privacy and safety of participants; reports harm.
  • Research utiliser / change agent – brings proven findings into protocols and policies.
  • Critic and reviewer – evaluates studies, reviews manuscripts, takes part in journal clubs.
  • Member of ethics or research committees.
  • Disseminator – presents and publishes findings; shares knowledge with colleagues.
  • Educator – teaches research and evidence-based practice to students.

(c) Research priority areas in nursing in India (5 marks)

Research priorities are areas where evidence is most needed to improve health and nursing services; they follow national health problems, national programmes and the Sustainable Development Goals.

  • Maternal and newborn health – PPH and anaemia, respectful maternity care, midwifery-led care, breastfeeding, KMC, newborn infection prevention, reduction of stillbirths.
  • Child and adolescent health – immunisation coverage, malnutrition and anaemia, adolescent health and menstrual hygiene.
  • Non-communicable diseases – hypertension and diabetes self-management, cancer screening (VIA, breast and oral), stroke rehabilitation, lifestyle interventions.
  • Communicable diseases and infection control – TB adherence, antimicrobial resistance, hospital-acquired infections, hand hygiene, dengue and malaria prevention.
  • Mental health – depression, suicide prevention, substance use, stress among nurses and students.
  • Geriatric and palliative care – falls, dementia care, pain and end-of-life care.
  • Community health – work of Community Health Officers at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, ASHA support, home-based care.
  • Nursing education – simulation, competency-based education, clinical teaching, e-learning.
  • Nursing administration and workforce – staffing norms, workload, burnout, job satisfaction, migration and retention, patient safety and quality indicators.
  • Digital health and innovations – telenursing, electronic records, artificial intelligence in nursing.
  • Disaster preparedness, climate change and occupational health of nurses.

(d) Brief explanation of important types

  • Descriptive research – describes the characteristics of a population or phenomenon as it exists (for example, "knowledge regarding cervical cancer among women"); no attempt to explain cause.
  • Exploratory research – investigates a new or little-known area to gain insight and generate hypotheses.
  • Explanatory and predictive research – explain why phenomena occur and predict outcomes from known factors (for example, factors predicting falls in the elderly).
  • Evaluative research – judges the effectiveness of a programme, policy or practice (for example, evaluation of a newly introduced bedside handover).
  • Cross-sectional versus longitudinal – a cross-sectional study collects data once from different people (quick and cheap); a longitudinal study follows the same people over time (shows change and sequence, but is costly and loses subjects).
  • Retrospective versus prospective – a retrospective study starts with an outcome and looks back for causes (for example, case records of women with eclampsia); a prospective study starts with a possible cause and follows people forward to observe outcomes.

(e) Qualities of a nurse researcher

  • Curiosity and a questioning attitude, critical thinking and creativity.
  • Honesty and integrity – no fabrication, falsification or plagiarism; respect for participants.
  • Knowledge of research methods and statistics, and willingness to learn.
  • Patience and perseverance, good time management.
  • Good communication and teamwork; ability to accept criticism.

(f) Barriers to research by nurses in India and ways to overcome them

  • Barriers – heavy workload and shortage of staff, lack of time, limited research training and mentoring, poor access to journals and databases, lack of funds and statistical support, lack of administrative support and recognition, fear of statistics, and language difficulties.
  • Ways forward – research cells and research committees in hospitals and colleges, journal clubs, protected time for research, collaborative and multidisciplinary studies, workshops on research methods and writing, use of open-access and institutional e-journal facilities, grants and awards for nurse researchers, and recognition of research in career progression.

(g) Research in the B.Sc. Nursing course – the group research project

  • In the seventh semester students carry out a small group research project under a teacher's guidance, to learn the research process by doing it.
  • Steps – choose a feasible problem from clinical or community practice → review literature → write objectives and hypotheses → select design and sample → prepare and validate the tool → obtain ethical permission and consent → pilot study → collect data → analyse with simple statistics → write the report → present it in the institution.
  • Roles within the group – a leader to coordinate, members sharing literature search, tool preparation, data collection, data entry and analysis, and writing.
  • Benefits – teamwork, critical thinking, statistical and writing skills, confidence in reading research, and a habit of evidence-based practice.

(h) How research priorities are decided

  • Priorities are set by considering the burden of the health problem, the gaps in existing evidence, the likely impact of the findings on patient outcomes and services, feasibility with available resources, and alignment with national health programmes, policies and the Sustainable Development Goals. Consultation with nurses, managers, teachers and patients makes the list realistic.

Nursing importance

  • Knowing the types of research, her own research role and national priorities helps the nurse choose meaningful, feasible studies that answer real problems of Indian patients and health services.

Conclusion Research can be classified by purpose, approach, design, objective, time and setting. Nurses at every level contribute to research, and directing studies to national priority areas makes nursing research useful for policy and practice.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the sources (ways) of acquiring knowledge in nursing and the place of the scientific method.
tags: limitations of scientific method in nursing
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses use knowledge from many sources to make decisions. Some sources are quick but unreliable; research based on the scientific method is the most dependable source, which is why it forms the foundation of evidence-based nursing.

1. Sources of knowledge

  • Tradition – "we have always done it this way" (for example, routine 4-hourly temperature recording); convenient but may continue outdated practices.
  • Authority – knowledge from experts, senior nurses, doctors and textbooks; useful but authorities can be wrong or out of date.
  • Borrowing – knowledge taken from other disciplines (medicine, psychology, sociology) and adapted to nursing.
  • Trial and error – trying alternatives until one works; risky and unsystematic, and results are rarely recorded.
  • Personal experience – learning from one's own clinical practice; valuable but limited and influenced by bias.
  • Intuition – an immediate understanding without conscious reasoning (expert nurses "sense" deterioration); difficult to explain or test.
  • Role modelling and mentorship – learning by observing and following experienced nurses.
  • Logical reasoning – inductive (from specific observations to a general conclusion) and deductive (from a general principle to a specific situation).
  • Research – systematic, scientific inquiry; the most reliable source, because it is objective, verifiable and open to correction.

2. The scientific method

  • Meaning – a set of orderly, systematic, controlled procedures for acquiring dependable, empirical information.
  • Steps – identify a problem → review existing knowledge → form a hypothesis → collect data by observation or experiment → analyse data → draw conclusions → report and verify.
  • Characteristics – order and control (systematic steps, control of extraneous factors), empiricism (evidence gathered through the senses and measurement), generalisation (findings applied beyond the sample), objectivity and verifiability.
  • Limitations in nursing – human beings are complex and unique; many nursing phenomena (comfort, hope, caring) are hard to measure; ethical limits prevent some experiments; complete control of human situations is not possible. Hence qualitative methods are also used.

3. An example from practice

  • Applying oil, egg white or spirit to pressure areas was long followed out of tradition; research showed that regular repositioning, pressure-redistributing mattresses, skin care and nutrition prevent pressure injuries – illustrating why research must replace untested tradition.

Conclusion Tradition, authority and experience are useful starting points, but nursing decisions should increasingly rest on knowledge produced by the scientific method and research.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Define nursing research.
answer_html:
• Nursing research is systematic inquiry designed to develop trustworthy evidence about issues of importance to the nursing profession, including nursing practice, education, administration and informatics (Polit and Beck).
  • Its purpose is to build nursing knowledge and to support evidence-based, high-quality care.
  • Example – a study to assess the effectiveness of chlorhexidine mouth care in preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia.
  • Unlike routine audits or problem-solving, research aims to produce new, generalisable knowledge using scientific methods.
  • It covers clinical practice, nursing education, administration and community health.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Differentiate between basic and applied research.
answer_html:
Basic (pure) research Applied research
Aims to extend knowledge and develop or test theory Aims to solve practical problems
No immediate practical application Findings have immediate use in practice
Often done in laboratory or controlled settings Done in real clinical or community settings
Example – studying the physiological basis of pain perception Example – effect of cold application on pain during IM injection
Results may take years to reach practice Results can be applied quickly

The two are complementary – basic research provides the theory that applied research tests in real settings.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is action research?
answer_html:
• Action research is research in which practitioners study a problem in their own setting and take action to solve it at the same time, with the participation of the people concerned.
  • It follows a repeated cycle of plan → act → observe → reflect, leading to practical change and improvement.
  • Example – ward nurses identify poor hand-hygiene compliance, introduce a reminder and audit system, measure compliance, and refine the system in further cycles.
  • Advantages – solves real local problems, involves staff and builds ownership of change; limitation – findings may not be generalisable to other settings.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: (a) Define research problem, problem statement and research question, and list the sources of research problems. (5 marks) (b) Explain the criteria for selecting a research problem. (5 marks) (c) Describe the steps of formulating a research problem, with an example of a problem statement. (5 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definitions and sources (5 marks)

Definitions

  • Research problem – a perplexing or troubling situation, a gap in knowledge, or an area of concern in nursing practice, education or administration that needs a solution through systematic inquiry.
  • Problem statement – a clear, concise statement of the problem to be studied, identifying the key variables, the population and the setting; it may be written in declarative form (title-like) or as a question.
  • Research question – a specific, answerable question that the researcher wants to answer through the study (for example, "What is the level of knowledge regarding kangaroo mother care among postnatal mothers?").

Sources of research problems

  • Clinical experience and nursing practice – daily problems such as falls, pressure injuries, pain, poor breastfeeding.
  • Review of literature – gaps, inconsistent findings and "recommendations for further research".
  • Theories – testing propositions of nursing or other theories.
  • Replication of earlier studies in a new population or setting.
  • Discussion with experts, teachers and colleagues, journal clubs, seminars and conferences.
  • National health problems and programmes, research priorities of funding agencies, and current social issues.
  • Problems in nursing education and administration – teaching methods, staffing, job satisfaction.
  • Concerns of patients and families, media reports.

(b) Criteria for selecting a research problem (5 marks)

1. The FINER criteria

  • F – Feasible – adequate number of subjects, technical expertise, time and money; manageable in scope.
  • I – Interesting – to the researcher, which sustains motivation.
  • N – Novel – adds new knowledge, confirms or extends earlier findings.
  • E – Ethical – can be done without harming participants and with their consent.
  • R – Relevant – important to nursing science, practice, policy or future research.

2. Other criteria

  • Significance to nursing – the findings should improve care, education or administration.
  • Researchability – the variables can be defined and measured; questions of value or morality ("Should euthanasia be legalised?") cannot be answered by research alone.
  • Researcher's qualifications and experience suited to the problem.
  • Availability and cooperation of subjects and permission from authorities.
  • Availability of facilities and resources – tools, equipment, library, statistical help.
  • Time and cost within the researcher's limits.
  • Clarity and precision of the problem.

(c) Steps of formulating a research problem (5 marks)

  1. Select a broad area of interest – for example, "breastfeeding" or "postnatal care".
  2. Review the literature and discuss with experts to learn what is known and where the gaps are.
  3. Narrow down (delimit) the topic – specify the aspect (knowledge of KMC), the population (postnatal mothers of low birth weight babies) and the setting (selected hospitals).
  4. Identify the variables – independent (for example, a structured teaching programme) and dependent (knowledge or practice), and demographic variables.
  5. Formulate the research question(s) and then the problem statement.
  6. Evaluate the problem against the selection criteria (feasibility, significance, ethics).
  7. State the objectives (and hypotheses where needed) and write operational definitions of the terms.

Example of a problem statement

  • "A study to assess the effectiveness of a structured teaching programme on knowledge regarding kangaroo mother care among postnatal mothers of low birth weight babies in selected hospitals."
  • Objectives – (1) to assess the pre-test knowledge of postnatal mothers regarding KMC; (2) to evaluate the effectiveness of the structured teaching programme by comparing pre-test and post-test knowledge scores; (3) to find the association between pre-test knowledge and selected demographic variables.
  • Hypotheses – H₁: the mean post-test knowledge score will be significantly higher than the mean pre-test score at p <0.05; H₂: there will be a significant association between pre-test knowledge and selected demographic variables.

(d) Forms of the problem statement

  • Declarative form – "A study to assess the knowledge regarding prevention of cervical cancer among women in a selected rural area."
  • Interrogative form – "What is the knowledge regarding prevention of cervical cancer among women in a selected rural area?"
  • Indian nursing theses commonly use the declarative form as the title and write the research questions separately.

(e) Writing the objectives

  • General objective – the broad aim of the study; specific objectives – the precise steps by which the aim will be achieved.
  • Good objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART) and begin with action verbs such as to assess, to determine, to identify, to compare, to evaluate, to find the association, to correlate.
  • Each objective should be answered by the analysis; avoid vague verbs such as to know or to understand.

(f) Writing the need for (significance of) the study

  • Show the magnitude of the problem with recent data (national surveys, WHO reports, hospital records).
  • Point out the gap in knowledge or practice found in the literature and in the researcher's experience.
  • Explain the consequences of not solving the problem and the expected benefits to patients, nurses and the health system.

(g) Common errors in formulating a research problem

  • A problem that is too broad ("health of women") or too narrow to be meaningful.
  • Value or moral questions that research cannot answer ("Should nurses prescribe?").
  • Vague, undefined terms, too many variables, or variables that cannot be measured.
  • Problems that are not feasible (no access to subjects, too costly) or unethical.
  • Repeating a well-answered question without a justification for replication.

(h) Assumptions, delimitations and limitations

  • Assumptions – basic beliefs accepted as true without testing, on which the study rests; for example, "postnatal mothers have some knowledge of newborn care" or "a structured teaching programme will improve knowledge".
  • Delimitations – boundaries deliberately set by the researcher to keep the study manageable; for example, "the study is delimited to postnatal mothers of low birth weight babies admitted to selected hospitals during the period of data collection".
  • Limitations – weaknesses outside the researcher's control that restrict generalisation, such as a small or non-random sample or a short follow-up; they are stated honestly in the report.

(i) Conceptual (theoretical) framework

  • A framework links the study's concepts in a logical structure, often based on a nursing or other theory (for example, the general system theory or Pender's health promotion model).
  • It explains how the variables are expected to relate, guides the hypotheses, tool and interpretation, and is usually shown as a diagram in the report.

(j) Example of research questions for a descriptive study

  • Problem – "A study to assess the knowledge regarding warning signs of cancer among adults in a selected community."
  • Research questions – (1) What is the level of knowledge regarding the warning signs of cancer among adults? (2) Is there an association between the knowledge and selected demographic variables such as age, education and occupation?
  • Each question is answered by a specific part of the analysis – frequency and percentage for the first, chi-square for the second.

Nursing importance

  • A clearly formulated, feasible and significant problem is half the research done; poorly framed problems lead to wasted effort and weak findings.

Conclusion A good research problem arises from practice, literature or theory, satisfies the FINER criteria, and is narrowed down step by step into a precise problem statement with clear objectives and hypotheses.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Define hypothesis. Explain its characteristics and types, with suitable examples.
answer_html:
Introduction A hypothesis is a tentative prediction or statement about the expected relationship between two or more variables in a population, which can be tested by research. It translates the research question into a precise prediction and guides the design, data collection and analysis.

1. Purposes

  • Gives direction to the study; links theory with observation.
  • Indicates the variables, the type of design and the statistical test.
  • Helps in interpreting results and drawing conclusions.

2. Characteristics of a good hypothesis

  • States a relationship between variables (independent and dependent).
  • Testable (empirically verifiable) – variables can be measured.
  • Clear, specific and concise, written in the present or future tense.
  • Consistent with existing knowledge and theory.
  • Identifies the population.
  • Plausible and simple; one prediction per hypothesis as far as possible.

3. Types with examples

Type Meaning Example
Simple One independent and one dependent variable Cold application reduces pain during IM injection
Complex Two or more independent and/or dependent variables Age, parity and education are related to knowledge and practice of breastfeeding
Directional Specifies the direction of the relationship Mothers who receive KMC teaching will have higher knowledge scores than those who do not
Non-directional States a relationship without direction There will be a difference in anxiety between primigravidae and multigravidae
Null hypothesis (H₀) – statistical States no relationship or no difference; it is what is tested statistically There is no significant difference between pre-test and post-test knowledge scores
Research / alternative hypothesis (H₁) States the expected relationship The post-test knowledge score will be significantly higher than the pre-test score
Associative Variables are related, without implying cause Body mass index is associated with blood pressure
Causal One variable causes a change in another Early ambulation reduces post-operative constipation

4. Testing – the null hypothesis is tested with a statistical test at a chosen level of significance (usually 0.05); it is rejected when p <0.05 (supporting the research hypothesis) or not rejected otherwise. A hypothesis is never "proved"; it is supported or not supported.

Conclusion A hypothesis is a testable prediction that gives direction to quantitative research; stating it clearly, with the correct type, makes analysis and interpretation straightforward.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Define variables. Explain the types of variables in research, with examples and operational definitions.
answer_html:
Introduction A variable is an attribute or characteristic of a person, object or situation that can take different values (for example age, weight, anxiety, knowledge, blood pressure). Identifying and defining variables precisely is essential for measurement and analysis.

1. Types of variables

  • Independent variable – the presumed cause, which the researcher manipulates or observes (for example, a structured teaching programme, warm compress, music therapy).
  • Dependent variable – the outcome or effect that is measured (for example, knowledge score, pain level, anxiety).
  • Extraneous (confounding) variables – other factors that can influence the dependent variable and distort results (for example, prior information from mass media, age, education); they must be controlled.
  • Demographic (attribute) variables – characteristics of subjects such as age, sex, education, religion, income, parity, place of residence; used to describe the sample and to find associations.
  • Research variables – in descriptive studies with no independent–dependent relationship, the variables simply measured (for example, "knowledge regarding cervical cancer").
  • Intervening (mediating) variable – comes between the independent and dependent variable and explains the relationship.
  • Moderator variable – changes the strength or direction of the relationship (for example, education affecting how well teaching works).

2. By nature of measurement

  • Continuous – can take any value in a range (weight, haemoglobin).
  • Discrete – whole numbers (number of children).
  • Categorical – categories (blood group, religion); dichotomous when only two (yes/no, male/female).

3. Conceptual and operational definitions

  • A conceptual definition gives the theoretical meaning (for example, "anxiety is a feeling of apprehension and tension").
  • An operational definition states exactly how the variable will be measured in the study – for example, "Knowledge refers to the correct responses of postnatal mothers to the structured knowledge questionnaire on KMC, measured by the knowledge score"; "Pain is the score reported on the 0–10 numerical rating scale".

4. Control of extraneous variables – random assignment, selecting a homogeneous sample, matching, using a control group, keeping the procedure constant, and statistical control (analysis of covariance).

5. Example in one study – in "effectiveness of music therapy on pre-operative anxiety among patients", music therapy is the independent variable, anxiety score the dependent variable, age and previous surgery are demographic variables, and noise in the ward or the surgeon's explanation are extraneous variables to be controlled.

Conclusion Clearly identified independent, dependent and extraneous variables, with precise operational definitions, make a study measurable, controlled and repeatable.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is a null hypothesis? Give an example.
answer_html:
• The null hypothesis (H₀) is a statistical hypothesis stating that there is no relationship between the variables or no difference between groups; any observed difference is due to chance.
  • It is the hypothesis that is tested by statistical tests; it is rejected when the p value is less than the chosen level of significance (usually 0.05), which supports the research (alternative) hypothesis.
  • Example – "There is no significant difference between the mean pre-test and post-test knowledge scores of postnatal mothers regarding kangaroo mother care."

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is an operational definition? Give an example.
tags: how variable is measured in the study
answer_html:
• An operational definition describes exactly how a term or variable is observed or measured in a particular study, in measurable terms, so that others can understand and repeat the study.
  • It differs from a conceptual (dictionary) definition, which gives only the general meaning.
  • Examples – "Effectiveness refers to the significant gain in knowledge scores after the structured teaching programme, measured by comparing pre-test and post-test scores"; "Anxiety is the score obtained on the modified state anxiety scale".
  • Operational definitions are written for all key terms of the problem statement (for example effectiveness, structured teaching programme, knowledge, postnatal mothers).

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is the PICOT format of a research question?
answer_html:
• PICOT is a format for writing a focused, searchable clinical research question:
    • P – Population/Patient (for example, post-caesarean mothers)
    • I – Intervention or issue (early ambulation)
    • C – Comparison (routine care)
    • O – Outcome (incidence of constipation or flatus time)
    • T – Time (within the first 48 hours)
  • Example – "In post-caesarean mothers (P), does early ambulation (I) compared with routine care (C) reduce the time to passage of flatus (O) within the first 48 hours (T)?"
  • A well-built PICOT question supplies the keywords for the literature search and points to the right design.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Define review of literature. Explain its purposes, sources and the steps of writing a review of literature.
answer_html:
Introduction Review of literature (ROL) is a critical summary of published and unpublished research and non-research literature on a selected topic. It shows what is already known, how it was studied, and what still needs to be studied, and it places the new study in the context of existing knowledge.

1. Purposes

  • To identify a research problem and gaps in knowledge; to refine and delimit the problem.
  • To avoid unnecessary duplication and to learn from the mistakes of earlier studies.
  • To develop the conceptual or theoretical framework.
  • To select a suitable design, sampling method, tools and statistical analysis.
  • To formulate hypotheses and operational definitions.
  • To interpret and discuss findings by comparing them with earlier studies.

2. Sources of literature

  • Primary sources – original reports written by the researchers themselves (journal research articles, theses and dissertations, conference papers).
  • Secondary sources – descriptions or summaries of studies by someone other than the original researcher (textbooks, review articles, encyclopaedias); useful for background but should not replace primary sources.
  • Tertiary sources – indexes, abstracts and bibliographies that help locate literature.
  • Print – nursing and medical journals (for example, the Nursing Journal of India), textbooks, government reports.
  • Electronic – databases such as PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, the Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, DOAJ, and Shodhganga (Indian theses); websites of WHO, MoHFW, ICMR, INC.
  • Grey literature – unpublished reports, theses, government documents, conference proceedings.

3. Steps of reviewing and writing the literature

  1. Identify key concepts and keywords (and their synonyms) from the problem statement.
  2. Search library catalogues and electronic databases, combining keywords with Boolean operators, and set limits (years, language, study type).
  3. Screen titles and abstracts for relevance; retrieve full texts.
  4. Read critically – note the purpose, design, sample, tools, findings, limitations and relevance of each study.
  5. Record and organise – note cards or a literature matrix; keep full reference details.
  6. Synthesise – group studies by themes or variables (not simply one after another), noting agreements, contradictions and gaps.
  7. Write – an introduction, organised themes (for example, "studies related to knowledge of KMC", "studies related to effectiveness of teaching programmes"), and a summary; paraphrase in your own words and cite every source to avoid plagiarism.
  8. Reference in a standard style (APA or Vancouver) consistently.

4. Qualities of a good review

  • Uses mainly recent primary research, is critical rather than merely descriptive, logically organised, unbiased (includes studies with contrary findings) and accurately referenced.

Conclusion A thorough, critical review of literature is the foundation of a good study – it sharpens the problem, guides the methodology and helps interpret the findings.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is an annotated bibliography?
answer_html:
• An annotated bibliography is a list of references (citations) to books, articles and documents, each followed by a brief descriptive and evaluative paragraph (the annotation) of about 100–200 words.
  • The annotation summarises the purpose, method, sample, main findings and relevance of the source to the researcher's study, and may comment on its quality.
  • It helps the researcher organise the literature, judge the value of each source and prepare the review of literature.
  • Each entry typically has four parts – citation, summary, evaluation and relevance to the present study.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Differentiate between primary and secondary sources of literature.
answer_html:
Primary source Secondary source
Original report written by the person who conducted the study Description or summary of a study written by someone else
Gives full detail of methods and results Gives limited detail, may contain the author's interpretation or errors
Examples – research articles in journals, theses and dissertations, conference papers Examples – textbooks, review articles, encyclopaedias, newspaper reports
Preferred for the review of literature Used for background and to locate primary sources

For example, an original study published in a nursing journal or a thesis on Shodhganga is a primary source; a textbook chapter summarising such studies is a secondary source.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Name two commonly used referencing styles and give the format of a journal reference in Vancouver style.
answer_html:
• Commonly used styles – APA (American Psychological Association) style, with author–date in-text citations written as (Author, Year), and Vancouver style, with numbered citations in the order of appearance (common in medical and nursing journals). Harvard style is also used.
  • Vancouver format for a journal article – Surname Initials, Surname Initials. Title of the article. Abbreviated journal name. Year;Volume(Issue):first page–last page.
  • In Vancouver style the citations appear in the text as numbers [1], [2], and the reference list is arranged in numerical order, not alphabetically; in APA style the list is alphabetical by first author.
  • Whichever style is chosen must be used consistently throughout the report.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: (a) Define research design; list its elements and classify research designs. (4 marks) (b) Explain the experimental research designs – true experimental, quasi-experimental and pre-experimental – with notations and examples. (8 marks) (c) Explain the threats to internal and external validity of experimental studies. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Experimental, quasi-experimental and pre-experimental designs in notation
labels: Table of design diagrams using R (random assignment)

O (observation/measurement) and X (intervention): true – R O1 X O2 / R O1 O2 (pre-test post-test control group); R X O / R O (post-test only); Solomon four-group (four rows); quasi – O1 X O2 / O1 O2 (non-equivalent control group); O1 O2 O3 X O4 O5 O6 (time series); pre-experimental – X O (one-shot case study); O1 X O2 (one-group pre-test post-test); X O / O (static group comparison)

answer_html:
(a) Definition, elements and classification (4 marks)

Definition

  • A research design is the overall plan or blueprint for obtaining answers to the research questions and testing the hypotheses; it specifies how the study will be structured, how subjects will be selected and grouped, how and when data will be collected and how they will be analysed, while controlling sources of error.

Elements of a research design

  • Research approach (quantitative, qualitative or mixed) and the specific design.
  • Setting of the study and the population.
  • Sample, sample size and sampling technique, with inclusion and exclusion criteria.
  • Variables – independent, dependent and extraneous – and how extraneous variables will be controlled.
  • Intervention (if any), tools and the data collection procedure with timing of measurements.
  • Plan for data analysis and ethical considerations.

Classification of research designs

Approach Designs
Quantitative – experimental True experimental (randomised controlled trial), quasi-experimental, pre-experimental
Quantitative – non-experimental Descriptive (survey, comparative, correlational, developmental – cross-sectional and longitudinal), exploratory, ex post facto, epidemiological (case–control, cohort)
Qualitative Phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography, historical, case study, narrative, action research
Mixed methods Concurrent, sequential explanatory and sequential exploratory designs

(b) Experimental research designs (8 marks)

Notation used – R = random assignment; O = observation or measurement (pre-test or post-test); X = intervention (treatment).

1. True experimental designs

Essential features – manipulation (the researcher introduces the intervention), control (a control group that does not receive it) and randomisation (subjects are randomly assigned to groups). They are the strongest designs for testing cause–effect relationships.

  • Pre-test post-test control group design
    • R O₁ X O₂ (experimental group)
    • R O₁ – O₂ (control group)
    • Both groups are measured before and after; only the experimental group receives X. Example – effect of foot reflexology on post-operative pain, with randomly assigned groups.
  • Post-test only control group design
    • R X O (experimental) / R – O (control)
    • Used when a pre-test may influence results or is impossible (for example, comparing post-operative infection rates with two dressing methods).
  • Solomon four-group design
    • R O₁ X O₂ / R O₁ – O₂ / R – X O₂ / R – – O₂
    • Combines the above two designs and measures the effect of the pre-test itself; strong but needs a large sample.
  • Factorial design – tests two or more interventions and their interaction at the same time (for example, music therapy and deep breathing in a 2 × 2 design).
  • Crossover design – the same subjects receive both treatments in random order, with a wash-out period, acting as their own controls.

Merits – strongest evidence of causality, high internal validity, control of extraneous variables. Demerits – often not feasible or ethical in nursing (it may be wrong to withhold care), artificial settings, costly, Hawthorne effect, attrition.

2. Quasi-experimental designs

Features – manipulation is present, but randomisation or a control group is lacking. Common in nursing because random assignment is often not possible in wards and communities.

  • Non-equivalent control group pre-test post-test design
    • O₁ X O₂ (experimental group, for example ward A)
    • O₁ – O₂ (comparison group, ward B)
    • Groups are not randomly formed, so the pre-test is used to check their comparability. Example – effect of a planned teaching programme on knowledge of diabetic foot care, using two hospitals.
  • Time-series design
    • O₁ O₂ O₃ X O₄ O₅ O₆
    • Repeated measurements before and after the intervention in one group show trends (for example, monthly fall rates before and after a fall-prevention bundle).

Merits – practical and more feasible in real settings; ethical; some control. Demerits – weaker causal conclusions because groups may differ (selection bias) and other events may explain changes.

3. Pre-experimental designs

Features – little or no control; no randomisation and often no comparison group; the weakest designs, but widely used in student projects.

  • One-shot case study – X O (intervention, then a single measurement; no baseline).
  • One-group pre-test post-test design – O₁ X O₂ (most common in Indian nursing student studies; for example, "effectiveness of a structured teaching programme on knowledge regarding breast self-examination among college girls").
  • Static group comparison – X O / – O (a group that received the intervention is compared with one that did not, without pre-test or randomisation).

Merits – simple, quick, cheap, useful for pilot and educational studies. Demerits – cannot rule out other explanations (history, maturation, testing), so conclusions about effectiveness are tentative.

(c) Threats to internal and external validity (3 marks)

Internal validity – the extent to which the change in the dependent variable is truly due to the intervention. Threats:

  • History – outside events during the study (for example, a TV health programme on the same topic).
  • Maturation – natural changes in subjects with time (healing, growing older, learning).
  • Testing – the pre-test itself improves post-test scores.
  • Instrumentation – changes in the tool or the observer between measurements.
  • Selection bias – groups differ at the start.
  • Attrition (mortality) – loss of subjects during the study.
  • Statistical regression – extreme scores move towards the average on retesting.
  • Contamination – the control group learns about the intervention.

External validity – the extent to which findings can be generalised to other people, settings and times. Threats:

  • Hawthorne effect – subjects change their behaviour because they know they are being studied.
  • Reactive effect of the pre-test – the pre-test makes subjects more sensitive to the intervention.
  • Novelty and experimenter effects; unrepresentative samples and settings (interaction of selection and treatment).

Ways to reduce threats – randomisation, control groups, blinding, standard procedures and tools, short intervals, intention-to-treat analysis, and representative samples.

(d) Selecting an appropriate design

  • Nature of the research question – to describe a situation (descriptive survey), to relate variables (correlational), to compare groups (comparative), or to test the effect of an intervention (experimental or quasi-experimental).
  • Possibility of manipulation and randomisation – often limited in wards and communities, leading to quasi-experimental designs.
  • Ethical considerations – an effective treatment cannot be withheld from a control group; harmful exposures cannot be assigned.
  • Feasibility – number and accessibility of subjects, time, cost, facilities and the researcher's expertise.
  • Example – "effectiveness of a structured teaching programme on knowledge" in a single hospital usually uses a one-group pre-test post-test design; adding a similar group from another hospital makes it a non-equivalent control group design, and random allocation of mothers to groups makes it a true experiment.

Nursing importance

  • Choosing the right design – true experimental where feasible, quasi- or pre-experimental where not – and recognising its limitations allows nurses to judge how much confidence to place in a study's claim that an intervention works.

Conclusion The research design is the blueprint of a study. Experimental designs differ in the degree of manipulation, control and randomisation; the stronger the control, the more confidently cause and effect can be inferred, provided threats to validity are recognised and minimised.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the non-experimental research designs, with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction In non-experimental designs the researcher does not manipulate the independent variable; phenomena are observed, described and related as they naturally occur. They are used when manipulation is impossible or unethical (for example, smoking, age, illness) and form a large part of nursing research.

1. Descriptive designs

  • Univariate descriptive (survey) – describes the characteristics, knowledge, attitudes or practices of a group, often by questionnaire or interview. Example – "a study to assess the knowledge regarding menstrual hygiene among adolescent girls in a selected school."
  • Comparative descriptive – compares two or more groups on a variable. Example – "a comparative study on stress among nurses working in ICUs and general wards."
  • Correlational – examines the relationship between two or more variables without implying cause. Example – "correlation between BMI and blood pressure among adults"; analysed by correlation coefficients.
  • Developmental designs – study change over time:
    • Cross-sectional – data from different age groups at one time (quick, cheap).
    • Longitudinal – the same group followed over a period (cohort, trend and panel studies); shows change and sequence but is costly and subject to drop-outs.

2. Exploratory design

  • Used to investigate a new or poorly understood problem, to gain insight and generate hypotheses (for example, "factors influencing late booking of antenatal care in a tribal area").

3. Ex post facto (causal comparative) design

  • The effect has already occurred; the researcher looks back to find possible causes, by comparing groups with and without the outcome (for example, "factors associated with low birth weight among mothers delivered in a district hospital").

4. Epidemiological designs – case–control (starts with cases and controls, looks back at exposure) and cohort (starts with exposed and unexposed groups, follows them forward) – also non-experimental.

5. Merits and limitations

  • Merits – suitable when experiments are impossible or unethical; studies variables in natural settings; can study many variables; relatively quick and economical (especially surveys); useful for describing problems and planning services.
  • Limitations – cannot establish cause and effect; risk of self-report bias and confounding; descriptive results may be superficial.

Conclusion Non-experimental designs – descriptive, correlational, developmental, exploratory and ex post facto – describe and relate phenomena as they exist, providing much of the basic evidence on which nursing interventions are later tested.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the qualitative research designs – phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography and case study.
answer_html:
Introduction Qualitative research studies human experiences, meanings and behaviour in their natural settings, using narrative data (words, observations) rather than numbers. It answers "what is it like?" and "why?" questions that numbers cannot capture – very relevant to nursing, which deals with the human experience of illness. Common features are small purposive samples, collection until data saturation, simultaneous data collection and analysis, and thematic analysis.

1. Phenomenology

  • Aim – to describe and understand the lived experience of a phenomenon as experienced by the people themselves (rooted in the philosophy of Husserl and Heidegger).
  • Method – in-depth, unstructured interviews with a few participants who have lived the experience; the researcher "brackets" (sets aside) personal beliefs; statements are analysed for essential themes.
  • Example – "lived experiences of mothers whose babies are admitted in an NICU."

2. Grounded theory

  • Aim – to generate a theory about a social process that is "grounded" in the data (developed by Glaser and Strauss).
  • Method – interviews and observation; theoretical sampling (choosing participants to develop emerging concepts); constant comparative analysis; coding (open, axial, selective) leading to a core category and a theoretical model.
  • Example – "the process of adjusting to life on haemodialysis."

3. Ethnography

  • Aim – to describe and interpret the culture – beliefs, values, practices – of a group (Leininger's ethnonursing applies it to nursing).
  • Method – prolonged fieldwork, participant observation, interviews with key informants, field notes and documents.
  • Example – "traditional postnatal practices among women of a tribal community."

4. Case study

  • Aim – an in-depth, intensive study of a single unit – a person, family, ward, institution or community – often over time, using several data sources.
  • Example – "a case study of a community's response to a dengue outbreak."

5. Ensuring quality (trustworthiness) – Lincoln and Guba's criteria: credibility (member checking, prolonged engagement), dependability (audit trail), confirmability (reflexivity), and transferability (thick description).

6. Merits and limitations

  • Merits – rich, deep understanding; gives voice to patients; generates hypotheses and theories; suits sensitive and complex topics.
  • Limitations – small samples limit generalisation; time-consuming; subjective interpretation; requires skilled interviewers and analysts.

Conclusion Phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography and case study offer different ways to explore human experience; with careful attention to trustworthiness, they provide insights that strengthen holistic nursing care.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain historical research – its sources, steps and the criticism of data.
answer_html:
Introduction Historical research is the systematic collection, critical evaluation and interpretation of data about past events, to understand the present and plan for the future. In nursing it helps trace the development of the profession, its education, practices and leaders.

1. Purposes

  • To understand how and why present practices developed; to learn from past successes and mistakes.
  • To build professional identity and pride.
  • To guide policy and future planning.
  • Example topics – "the development of nursing education in India after Independence", "the contribution of Florence Nightingale to hospital sanitation", "history of the midwife in a region".

2. Sources of data

  • Primary sources – first-hand evidence created at the time: original documents, government orders, minutes of meetings, hospital records, letters, diaries, photographs, uniforms and equipment (relics), and oral history interviews with people who witnessed the events.
  • Secondary sources – accounts written later by people who were not witnesses – books, articles and biographies; used for background but checked against primary sources.

3. Steps

  1. Selecting and defining the topic – clear in time period, place and focus.
  2. Reviewing the literature to see what has already been written.
  3. Locating and collecting data from archives, libraries, institutions and individuals.
  4. Criticism (evaluation) of data:
    • External criticism – tests the authenticity (genuineness) of the source: Is it what it claims to be? Who wrote it, when and where? Is it original or a forgery?
    • Internal criticism – tests the accuracy and trustworthiness of the content: Was the author in a position to know? Was he biased? Is it consistent with other sources?
  5. Analysis and synthesis – organising facts in chronological or thematic order and identifying patterns and causes.
  6. Interpretation and writing the report, with full references to sources.

4. Merits and limitations

  • Merits – the only way to study past events; provides context and perspective; inexpensive in equipment.
  • Limitations – records may be incomplete, lost or biased; events cannot be repeated or tested; the researcher's interpretation may introduce bias; time-consuming.

5. Example of criticism

  • A letter said to be written by an early nursing superintendent is checked for paper, ink, handwriting, date and signature against known documents (external criticism); its statements about student numbers are then compared with the hospital's annual reports of the same year (internal criticism).

Conclusion Historical research, with careful external and internal criticism of primary sources, reconstructs the past of nursing and gives valuable lessons for its present and future.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is randomisation in research?
answer_html:
• Randomisation (random assignment) is the allocation of subjects to the experimental and control groups by chance, so that every subject has an equal chance of being placed in either group.
  • Methods – lottery (chit) method, random number table, computer-generated random sequence; allocation concealed in sealed envelopes.
  • Purpose – distributes known and unknown extraneous variables equally between groups and removes selection bias, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the intervention.
  • It is different from random sampling, which concerns selection of the sample from the population.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is mixed-methods research? Name its basic designs.
answer_html:
• Mixed-methods research is a study in which the investigator collects, analyses and integrates both quantitative and qualitative data within a single study, so that the strengths of one approach make up for the limitations of the other.
  • Basic designs – convergent (parallel) – both kinds of data collected at the same time and compared; explanatory sequential – quantitative first, then qualitative to explain the results; exploratory sequential – qualitative first, then a quantitative phase (for example, developing a tool); embedded – one type supports the other within a trial.
  • Example – a survey of breastfeeding practices followed by in-depth interviews with mothers on the barriers they face.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is blinding? Name its types.
answer_html:
• Blinding (masking) is the practice of keeping people involved in a study unaware of which group (experimental or control) each subject belongs to, in order to prevent bias in behaviour, reporting and measurement.
  • Types
    • Single-blind – the subjects do not know their group.
    • Double-blind – both subjects and investigators/caregivers do not know.
    • Triple-blind – subjects, investigators and the data analyst (or outcome assessor) are all unaware.
  • A study in which everyone knows the allocation is called open-label.
  • Example – in a trial of a herbal mouthwash, the control group receives a placebo of the same colour, taste and bottle, so that neither patients nor nurses can tell the groups apart.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is triangulation in research?
answer_html:
• Triangulation is the use of more than one method, source, investigator or theory to study the same phenomenon, so that the findings are confirmed from different angles.
  • Types – data triangulation (different sources, times or places), investigator triangulation (more than one researcher), theory triangulation (different theoretical perspectives) and method triangulation (for example, interviews plus observation plus questionnaires).
  • It increases the credibility and completeness of findings, especially in qualitative and mixed-methods research.
  • Example – studying the experience of caregivers of stroke patients through interviews, home observation and caregiver diaries.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: (a) Define population, sample and sampling, and explain the characteristics of a good sample. (4 marks) (b) Explain the probability sampling techniques, with their merits and demerits. (5 marks) (c) Explain the non-probability sampling techniques. (4 marks) (d) Explain the factors determining sample size and the sampling errors. (2 marks)

diagram.caption: Classification of sampling techniques
labels: consecutive); with small pictorial examples – lottery chits
every k-th house on a list

answer_html:
(a) Definitions and characteristics of a good sample (4 marks)

Definitions

  • Population – the entire aggregation of people, objects or events that meet the criteria the researcher is interested in (for example, all postnatal mothers in a district).
    • Target population – the whole population to which results are to be generalised.
    • Accessible population – the part of the target population that the researcher can actually reach (postnatal mothers in the selected hospitals during the study period).
  • Sample – a subset of the population selected to participate in the study; each member is an element or subject.
  • Sampling – the process of selecting a portion of the population to represent the entire population.
  • Sampling frame – the list of all elements of the accessible population from which the sample is drawn (for example, a register of eligible couples).
  • Inclusion and exclusion criteria – characteristics that subjects must have (for example, mothers of babies weighing less than 2,500 g, able to read Marathi or Hindi) or must not have (critically ill mothers) to be eligible.

Why sampling is done – it saves time, money and effort; allows more careful data collection; studying the whole population is often impossible; and destructive tests cannot be done on everyone.

Characteristics of a good sample

  • Representative of the population in its important characteristics.
  • Adequate in size to give reliable results and detect real differences.
  • Selected by an appropriate, unbiased technique, preferably probability sampling.
  • Free from bias, feasible and economical; elements are accessible and willing.

(b) Probability sampling techniques (5 marks)

In probability sampling, every element of the population has a known, non-zero (often equal) chance of being selected; it allows generalisation and the use of inferential statistics.

1. Simple random sampling

  • Every element has an equal chance; selection by lottery (chit) method, random number table or computer-generated numbers from the sampling frame.
  • Merits – most unbiased; easy to understand. Demerits – needs a complete list; sample may be scattered; may miss small sub-groups.

2. Systematic sampling

  • Every k-th element is chosen from a list after a random start, where the sampling interval k = population size ÷ sample size (for example, from 500 houses, a sample of 50 → every 10th house after a random start between 1 and 10).
  • Merits – simple and quick; spreads the sample evenly. Demerits – bias if the list has a periodic pattern.

3. Stratified random sampling

  • The population is divided into homogeneous sub-groups (strata) – by age, sex, religion, ward or year of study – and a random sample is drawn from each stratum, proportionately (in proportion to stratum size) or disproportionately.
  • Merits – ensures representation of every sub-group; more precise; allows comparison between strata. Demerits – needs knowledge of strata; more complex.

4. Cluster (area) and multistage sampling

  • The population is divided into naturally occurring groups (clusters) – villages, schools, wards – and whole clusters are selected randomly; in multistage sampling random selection is done in stages (districts → blocks → villages → households), as in NFHS.
  • Merits – practical and economical for large, scattered populations; no complete list of individuals needed. Demerits – higher sampling error; clusters may differ from one another.

(c) Non-probability sampling techniques (4 marks)

In non-probability sampling, elements are selected by non-random methods; the chance of selection is unknown, so representativeness and generalisation are limited – but these methods are convenient and widely used in nursing studies.

  • Convenience (accidental) sampling – the most readily available subjects are taken (for example, patients attending the OPD on the days of data collection). Easy and cheap, but most prone to bias.
  • Purposive (judgemental) sampling – the researcher deliberately selects subjects who are typical or knowledgeable about the topic (for example, mothers of babies in KMC); used widely in student projects and qualitative research.
  • Quota sampling – the researcher fixes quotas for sub-groups (for example, 30 men and 30 women, or proportionate numbers from each age group) and fills them by convenience; improves representation over convenience sampling but is still non-random.
  • Snowball (network) sampling – initial subjects refer other subjects who share the characteristic; useful for hidden or hard-to-reach groups (drug users, survivors of violence, transgender persons).
  • Consecutive sampling – every eligible subject is enrolled in sequence until the sample size is reached (a better form of convenience sampling, common in hospital studies).
Point Convenience sampling Quota sampling
Basis Whoever is available Pre-fixed numbers from each sub-group, then available subjects
Representation Poor Better, as sub-groups are represented
Bias High Moderate

(d) Sample size and sampling errors (2 marks)

Factors determining sample size

  • Type of study and design (experimental studies may need fewer; surveys need more); number of variables and sub-groups.
  • Expected effect size – smaller differences need larger samples; homogeneity of the population.
  • Desired precision (margin of error), level of significance and power.
  • Expected attrition, time, cost and availability of subjects.
  • Example of a formula for estimating a proportion – n = Z²pq ÷ d²; with Z = 1.96 (95% confidence), p = 50% (q = 50%) and an absolute error d = 10%, n = 3.84 × 0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 0.01 ≈ 96.

Sampling errors

  • Sampling error – the difference between the sample value (statistic) and the true population value (parameter) that arises because only a part of the population is studied; reduced by larger and properly random samples.
  • Non-sampling errors – errors from faulty tools, non-response, interviewer bias, recording and data entry mistakes; reduced by good tools, training and checking.
  • Sampling bias – systematic over- or under-representation of some groups due to faulty selection.

(e) Steps of the sampling process

  1. Define the target population clearly (who, where, when).
  2. Identify the accessible population and prepare or obtain the sampling frame.
  3. Lay down the inclusion and exclusion criteria.
  4. Choose the sampling technique suited to the design and resources.
  5. Decide the sample size (formula, power analysis or previous studies), adding a margin for drop-outs.
  6. Select the subjects, obtain informed consent and record reasons for refusals.
  7. Take measures to reduce attrition and to document the final sample accurately.

(f) Sampling in qualitative research

  • Qualitative studies use purposive, snowball or theoretical sampling to select information-rich participants who have experienced the phenomenon.
  • Sample size is small (often about 6–20) and is not fixed in advance – data collection continues until data saturation, when new interviews no longer add new themes.

Nursing importance

  • The value of any study depends on whom it studied. A nurse researcher who selects an adequate, representative sample with a suitable technique – and who honestly reports its limitations – produces findings that can be trusted and applied.

Conclusion Sampling allows study of a manageable portion of the population. Probability methods give representative samples suitable for generalisation, while non-probability methods are practical for many nursing and qualitative studies; adequate sample size and awareness of sampling errors are essential.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: (a) Define data collection and list the methods and tools of data collection. (4 marks) (b) Explain the questionnaire method – types of questions, steps of construction, merits and demerits. (6 marks) (c) Explain the interview method – types, techniques, merits and demerits – and the ethical considerations during data collection. (5 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition, methods and tools (4 marks)

Definition

  • Data collection is the systematic gathering of information relevant to the research problem, using methods and tools appropriate to the variables and the population.
  • Primary data are collected first-hand by the researcher; secondary data are taken from existing records (hospital records, HMIS, census, NFHS).

Methods and tools

Method Tools (instruments)
Self-report (written) Questionnaire – knowledge, attitude, practice; scales – Likert attitude scale, anxiety and depression scales
Self-report (verbal) Interview schedule (structured), interview guide (semi-/unstructured), focus group guide
Observation Checklist, rating scale, anecdotal records, field notes, audio/video recording
Biophysiological measures BP apparatus, thermometer, glucometer, pulse oximeter, weighing scale, laboratory tests
Records and documents Case records, registers, partographs, death certificates
Others Projective techniques, Q-sort, semantic differential scale, vignettes, Delphi technique (consensus of experts through rounds of questionnaires)

The choice depends on the research question, type of variables, characteristics of subjects (literacy, age), setting, time and cost.

(b) Questionnaire method (6 marks)

Meaning – a questionnaire is a printed or electronic set of questions that the respondent answers by himself or herself (self-administered).

Types of questions

  • Open-ended – the respondent answers in his own words ("What problems did you face during breastfeeding?"); gives rich information but is difficult to analyse.
  • Closed-ended (fixed-alternative):
    • Dichotomous – two options (yes/no, true/false).
    • Multiple choice – one correct answer among several (common in knowledge questionnaires).
    • Rating (Likert-type) – strongly agree to strongly disagree.
    • Ranking – arranging options in order of preference.
    • Checklist – ticking all that apply.

Steps in constructing a questionnaire

  1. Define the purpose and the variables; review literature and existing tools.
  2. Prepare a blueprint – the areas (domains) to be covered, number of items per area and their weight, and the type of items.
  3. Write the items – simple, clear, unambiguous language; one idea per question; avoid leading, double-barrelled, negative and embarrassing questions; avoid technical jargon.
  4. Arrange the items – from general to specific and easy to difficult; group by topic; demographic data at the beginning (or end); sensitive questions later.
  5. Prepare instructions and a scoring key (for example, 1 mark for each correct answer; knowledge graded as adequate, moderately adequate, inadequate).
  6. Establish content validity by giving the tool to experts; modify as suggested.
  7. Translation and back-translation into the local language (Marathi, Hindi) by language experts.
  8. Pre-test (try-out) on a few similar subjects and check reliability; finalise the tool.

Merits – economical in time and money; can cover a large, scattered sample; anonymity encourages honest answers; uniform questions; no interviewer bias; easy to analyse closed questions. Demerits – cannot be used with illiterate respondents or young children; low response rate (postal/online); questions may be misunderstood with no chance to clarify; no control over who fills it; respondents may consult others; superficial answers.

(c) Interview method and ethical considerations (5 marks)

Meaning – an interview is a face-to-face (or telephonic/online) verbal interaction in which the interviewer asks questions and records the responses.

Types

  • Structured interview – a fixed interview schedule with questions asked in the same order and words to every respondent; suitable for quantitative studies and illiterate subjects.
  • Semi-structured interview – an interview guide of key questions with freedom to probe.
  • Unstructured (in-depth) interview – conversation around a broad topic; used in qualitative research.
  • Focus group discussion – a moderated discussion with 6–10 similar participants on a topic.
  • Telephone and online (video) interviews.

Interview techniques

  • Plan the time and place; obtain consent; ensure privacy and comfort.
  • Build rapport – introduce yourself, explain the purpose, assure confidentiality.
  • Ask questions clearly and neutrally; listen actively; probe for clarification without leading.
  • Record accurately (notes or audio recording with permission).
  • Close politely, thank the respondent and check that nothing important is missed.

Merits – usable with illiterate people, children and the elderly; high response rate; questions can be clarified; non-verbal cues observed; in-depth information obtained. Demerits – time-consuming and costly; interviewer bias; respondents may give socially desirable answers; lack of anonymity; requires trained interviewers.

Ethical considerations during data collection

  • Approval from the institutional ethics committee and permission from the authorities of the setting.
  • Informed consent – explain the purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, time required and voluntary nature; written consent (thumb impression with a witness for illiterate subjects); assent plus parental consent for minors.
  • Voluntary participation and the right to withdraw at any time without loss of care.
  • Confidentiality and anonymity – codes instead of names; safe storage of data.
  • Privacy for sensitive questions and physical examinations.
  • No harm – avoid physical, psychological, social or economic harm; extra protection for vulnerable groups.
  • Honesty – no fabrication of data or "filling" of questionnaires by the investigator.

(d) Questionnaire compared with interview

Point Questionnaire Interview
Literacy needed Yes No
Cost and time Low; large samples possible High; smaller samples
Response rate Often low (postal, online) High
Clarification of questions Not possible Possible; probing allowed
Anonymity Greater, so more honest on sensitive issues Less
Interviewer bias Absent May be present
Depth of information Limited Greater

(e) Biophysiological measures

  • In vivo measures are taken directly on the person (BP, pulse, temperature, SpO₂, weight, peak flow); in vitro measures use specimens (blood glucose, haemoglobin, urine tests).
  • Merits – objective, precise and valid; difficult for subjects to distort.
  • Demerits – equipment cost, need for skill, possible discomfort or risk, and errors from faulty equipment.
