  • Nurse's role – use calibrated, standardised equipment, follow the same procedure and timing for every subject, train data collectors and record readings immediately.

(f) Common problems during data collection and their solutions

  • Non-availability or refusal of subjects – flexible timing, clear explanation, respect for refusal.
  • Interruptions in wards and homes – choose suitable times, arrange privacy.
  • Incomplete or wrongly filled tools – check each tool on the spot before leaving.
  • Loss of subjects for the post-test – collect contact details, give reminders, plan short intervals.

(g) Choosing the method of data collection – factors

  • Nature of the variable – knowledge and attitudes are best measured by questionnaires or scales, practices by observation (what people do may differ from what they say), and physiological outcomes by biophysiological measures.
  • Characteristics of the subjects – literacy, age, language, illness, ability to communicate.
  • Sensitivity of the topic – anonymous questionnaires suit sensitive subjects; skilled interviews suit complex experiences.
  • Setting, time, cost and the researcher's skill.
  • Many studies combine methods – for example, an interview schedule for knowledge with an observation checklist for practice – which strengthens the findings.

Nursing importance

  • The quality of research data depends on good tools and careful, ethical collection; nurses, who are skilled communicators, make effective interviewers when trained to avoid bias.

Conclusion Questionnaires and interviews are the most common self-report methods. Careful construction, validation and pre-testing of tools, skilled interviewing and strict ethical practice ensure accurate and trustworthy data.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain observation as a method of data collection, with the tools used.
answer_html:
Introduction Observation is a method of collecting data by watching and recording the behaviour, events, conditions or characteristics of people and situations in a systematic way. It is especially valuable in nursing, where many practices (hand hygiene, communication, procedures, patient behaviour) are best studied by watching rather than asking.

1. Types of observation

  • Structured – the researcher knows exactly what to observe and uses a checklist or rating scale; unstructured – the researcher observes and records everything relevant in field notes (qualitative).
  • Participant – the observer takes part in the activities of the group (ethnography); non-participant – the observer stays outside the activity.
  • Overt (disclosed) – subjects know they are observed; covert (concealed) – subjects are unaware (raises ethical issues, used only with ethics committee approval).
  • Natural setting or controlled (laboratory/simulation) setting.
  • Time sampling (observing at fixed intervals) and event sampling (observing whenever a particular event occurs).

2. Tools of observation

  • Checklist – a list of behaviours or steps recorded as present/absent or done/not done (for example, a checklist on the steps of hand washing or of AMTSL).
  • Rating scale – records the degree or quality of a behaviour:
    • Graphic rating scale – a line with descriptive points.
    • Numerical rating scale – for example 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent).
    • Descriptive rating scale – each level described in words.
  • Anecdotal records, field notes and diaries.
  • Audio and video recordings and mechanical devices (with consent).

3. Merits

  • Gives first-hand, direct information on actual behaviour rather than reported behaviour.
  • Useful with subjects who cannot respond verbally – infants, unconscious, mentally ill patients.
  • Studies behaviour in natural settings; complements other methods.

4. Demerits and sources of error

  • Time-consuming and costly; only observable behaviour can be studied (not feelings or past events).
  • Observer bias – personal expectations colour what is recorded; halo effect (a general impression influencing all ratings); Hawthorne effect in subjects.
  • Ethical problems with covert observation.

5. Improving accuracy – clear operational definitions of behaviours, training of observers, structured tools, checking inter-rater reliability (two observers recording the same event independently), and an adaptation period before recording.

Conclusion Observation, using well-designed checklists and rating scales and trained observers, provides direct and objective data on nursing practices and patient behaviour.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Define validity and reliability of a research tool. Explain their types and the methods of establishing them.
tags: measuring what it is intended to measure
answer_html:
Introduction The quality of research findings depends on the quality of the tools used. Two essential properties of a good tool are validity and reliability.

1. Validity

  • Definition – the degree to which a tool measures what it is intended to measure (accuracy).
  • Types
    • Face validity – the tool appears to measure the concept, judged superficially by experts and subjects.
    • Content validity – the tool adequately covers all the areas (content) of the concept, established by giving the tool and its blueprint to a panel of subject experts (often 5–7) who judge each item for relevance, clarity and adequacy; a content validity index (CVI) may be calculated. This is the commonest method in nursing student studies.
    • Criterion-related validity – the tool's scores are compared with an external standard (criterion): concurrent (with a criterion measured at the same time) or predictive (with a future outcome, for example, a fall-risk score predicting falls).
    • Construct validity – the tool truly measures the theoretical construct (anxiety, self-esteem); established by factor analysis, known-groups technique and correlation with related measures.

2. Reliability

  • Definition – the consistency or stability of a tool – the degree to which it gives the same results on repeated measurement under similar conditions.
  • Types and methods
    • Stability – test–retest method – the same tool is given to the same subjects twice, about 1–2 weeks apart, and the scores are correlated.
    • Internal consistency – the items measure the same concept:
    • Split-half method – items are divided into two halves (odd and even), the two half-scores are correlated, and the Spearman–Brown formula gives the reliability of the whole tool.
    • Cronbach's alpha (and KR-20 for right/wrong items).
    • Equivalence – inter-rater (inter-observer) reliability, when two observers rate the same event using the same tool, and parallel (alternate) forms.
  • A reliability coefficient of about 0.7 or above is generally considered acceptable (0.8 or more for important decisions).

3. Relationship – a tool can be reliable without being valid (consistently measuring the wrong thing), but cannot be valid unless it is reliable.

4. Improving validity and reliability – clear and unambiguous items, adequate number of items, clear instructions and scoring, expert review, pre-testing, trained data collectors and standard conditions of administration.

Conclusion Validity ensures that a tool measures the right thing and reliability ensures that it measures consistently; establishing both before the main study is essential for trustworthy results.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is a pilot study? Explain its purposes and the planning of data collection for the main study.
answer_html:
Introduction A pilot study is a small-scale trial run of the main study, carried out on a few subjects similar to those of the main study and in a similar setting, before the actual data collection, to test the feasibility of the plan.

1. Purposes

  • To find out the feasibility of the study – availability and cooperation of subjects, permission, time and cost.
  • To test the tool – clarity of language and instructions, time taken, difficulty of items – and to establish its reliability.
  • To test the intervention (for example, the structured teaching programme) and the procedure.
  • To identify practical problems in data collection and solve them in advance.
  • To check the methods of analysis and help estimate the sample size.
  • To give the researcher experience and confidence.

2. Conduct of a pilot study

  • Obtain permission; select about 10% of the main sample size (for example, 6 subjects for a main study of 60) by the same sampling technique, from a similar but separate setting.
  • Collect data exactly as planned; note the time taken and difficulties; analyse the data.
  • Modify the tool or procedure if needed; pilot subjects are not included in the main study.

3. Planning data collection for the main study

  • Formal permission from the institutional authorities and ethics committee approval.
  • Schedule – dates, days, time of day and duration of data collection (for example, four weeks).
  • Preparation – printed tools, consent forms, teaching aids, equipment; training of any data collectors.
  • Procedure – self-introduction and explanation of purpose → informed consent → pre-test (for example, 30 minutes) → intervention (STP of 45 minutes with AV aids) → post-test after the planned interval (for example, day 7) → thanking the participants.
  • Recording – coding of each tool, checking completeness at once, maintaining a master sheet.
  • Anticipating problems – non-availability of subjects, drop-outs, interruptions in the ward – and planning solutions.

4. Pilot study and pre-testing of the tool – the difference

  • Pre-testing (try-out) checks only the tool – its language, clarity and time required – on a few subjects.
  • A pilot study tests the whole study plan – sampling, intervention, tool, data collection procedure and analysis – on a small scale; the tool's reliability is often established during the pilot study.

Conclusion A pilot study is a rehearsal that reveals weaknesses before resources are spent on the main study; together with a carefully planned data collection procedure, it ensures smooth and valid data collection.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Define sampling error.
answer_html:
• Sampling error is the difference between a value obtained from the sample (statistic) and the true value in the population (parameter), which occurs because only a part of the population is studied.
  • It arises by chance, even with correct random sampling, and is measured by the standard error.
  • It is reduced by increasing the sample size and using proper probability sampling.
  • It differs from non-sampling errors, which arise from faulty tools, non-response, bias and recording mistakes.
  • Example – if the true mean haemoglobin of all antenatal women in a block is 10.5 g/dl and a sample shows 10.2 g/dl, the difference of 0.3 g/dl is the sampling error.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is snowball sampling?
answer_html:
• Snowball (network or chain-referral) sampling is a non-probability technique in which the first few subjects who meet the criteria help the researcher to identify and recruit other similar subjects, so the sample grows like a rolling snowball.
  • It is useful for hidden or hard-to-reach groups – injecting drug users, sex workers, survivors of violence, people with a stigmatised illness.
  • Merit – reaches subjects who could not otherwise be found; demerit – the sample may be biased because members tend to know similar people, so findings are not generalisable.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is a Likert scale?
answer_html:
• A Likert scale (developed by Rensis Likert, 1932) is a summated rating scale used to measure attitudes and opinions.
  • It consists of a series of statements about the topic, each with usually five response options – strongly agree, agree, undecided, disagree, strongly disagree – scored 5 to 1 for positive statements and reversed (1 to 5) for negative statements.
  • The scores of all items are added to give a total attitude score; higher scores show a more favourable attitude.
  • Example – "Breastfeeding should be started within one hour of birth." (SA / A / U / D / SD).

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is a visual analogue scale (VAS)?
answer_html:
• A visual analogue scale (VAS) is a tool for measuring subjective experiences such as pain, anxiety, fatigue or nausea.
  • It is a straight line, usually 100 mm long, with anchor words at each end (for example, "no pain" at 0 and "worst possible pain" at 100).
  • The subject marks a point on the line that represents his or her feeling; the distance from the zero end, measured in millimetres, is the score.
  • It is simple, quick and sensitive to change, but needs good vision and understanding; numerical and faces rating scales are alternatives.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is a sampling frame?
tags: list of all elements of accessible population
answer_html:
• A sampling frame is the actual list of all the elements (units) of the accessible population from which the sample is drawn.
  • Examples – the eligible couple register of a sub-centre, an admission register of a hospital ward, a school's list of students, a voter list.
  • It is essential for probability sampling methods such as simple random and systematic sampling.
  • An incomplete or outdated frame (missing names, duplicate entries) introduces sampling bias, so the frame should be checked and updated before sampling.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the steps in the analysis of research data – compilation, editing, coding, classification, tabulation, summarisation, presentation and interpretation.
answer_html:
Introduction Data analysis is the systematic organisation and synthesis of research data and, in quantitative studies, the testing of hypotheses using statistics. Raw data have no meaning until they are compiled, organised, summarised and interpreted in relation to the objectives.

Steps in data analysis

  1. Compilation – gathering all filled tools and records in one place; numbering each tool.
  2. Editing – checking each tool for completeness, accuracy, consistency and legibility; incomplete or doubtful responses are clarified with the subject (if possible) or excluded according to a rule.
  3. Coding – assigning numbers or symbols to responses (for example, male = 1, female = 2; correct answer = 1, wrong = 0) according to a code book, so that data can be counted and entered into a computer.
  4. Data entry and the master sheet – coded data of all subjects are entered in a master sheet (rows = subjects, columns = variables) on paper or in a spreadsheet (Excel) or statistical software; entry is double-checked.
  5. Classification – arranging data into groups or classes with common characteristics – by attributes (sex, religion, education) or by class intervals for numerical data (age groups, score ranges).
  6. Tabulation – presenting classified data systematically in rows and columns – frequency tables, cross-tables.
  7. Summarisation (statistical analysis)
    • Descriptive statistics – frequency, percentage, mean, median, mode, standard deviation – to describe the sample and the variables.
    • Inferential statistics – t-test, chi-square, correlation and others – to test hypotheses and generalise to the population.
  8. Presentation – tables, graphs and diagrams (bar diagram, pie chart, histogram, line graph) that make findings clear.
  9. Interpretation – explaining what the results mean in relation to the objectives and hypotheses, comparing them with earlier studies, noting unexpected findings and limitations, and drawing conclusions.

Qualitative data are analysed differently – transcribing interviews, reading repeatedly, coding meaningful units, grouping codes into categories and themes, and supporting themes with participants' quotations.

Common errors to avoid – analysing before checking data for errors, using tests unsuited to the level of data, reporting only percentages without numbers, ignoring missing data, and over-interpreting small differences. Spreadsheets and statistical software (Excel, SPSS, Epi Info, R) speed up analysis, but the researcher must still choose the right tests and interpret the output correctly.

Conclusion Systematic editing, coding, classification, tabulation, statistical summarisation, clear presentation and careful interpretation convert raw data into meaningful research findings.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain tabulation of data – the parts of a table, types of tables and the rules of tabulation.
answer_html:
Introduction Tabulation is the systematic arrangement of classified data in rows and columns. A well-prepared table condenses large data, allows quick comparison and forms the basis for statistical analysis and graphs.

1. Parts of a table

  • Table number – for identification and reference (Table 1, Table 2).
  • Title – brief and self-explanatory, stating what, who, where and when (for example, "Table 2: Frequency and percentage distribution of postnatal mothers according to their age, n = 60").
  • Captions (column headings) and stubs (row headings) – clear labels with units of measurement.
  • Body – the cells containing the numerical data.
  • Totals of rows and columns where appropriate.
  • Footnote – explanation of symbols, abbreviations or exceptions (for example, * significant at p <0.05).
  • Source note – where secondary data are used.

2. Types of tables

  • Simple (one-way) table – data classified by one characteristic (for example, distribution of subjects by age group).
  • Frequency distribution table – class intervals with their frequencies and percentages.
  • Complex tables – two-way (cross) tables or contingency tables showing two characteristics together (for example, knowledge level by education), used for the chi-square test; three-way tables for three characteristics.
  • Master table – summary of all the data of a study (usually in the appendix).

3. Rules of tabulation

  • Keep the table simple, clear and self-explanatory; avoid overcrowding – prepare several small tables rather than one large table.
  • Number and title every table; give units and totals.
  • Arrange data in a logical order (alphabetical, by size, chronological, or by categories of importance).
  • Give percentages alongside numbers, with the base (n) stated; round off consistently.
  • Place comparable figures close to each other; use lines to separate sections.
  • Mention the sample size (n) and the source; write the results in the text but do not repeat every number from the table.

4. Advantages of tabulation

  • Presents large data in a compact, orderly form that saves space and reading time.
  • Makes comparison between groups and categories easy.
  • Shows patterns, trends and errors in the data clearly.
  • Forms the basis for graphs and statistical calculations, and is easy to refer to in the report.

Conclusion A properly constructed table with a clear number, title, headings, body, totals and footnotes presents research data accurately and makes analysis and interpretation easier.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is coding of data?
tags: assigning numbers or symbols to responses
answer_html:
• Coding is the process of assigning numbers or symbols to the responses of research subjects so that the data can be counted, entered into a computer and analysed.
  • A code book records the code for every variable – for example, sex: male = 1, female = 2; education: illiterate = 0, primary = 1, secondary = 2, graduate = 3; knowledge item: correct = 1, wrong = 0.
  • Open-ended answers are first grouped into categories and then coded.
  • Coding should be consistent, exhaustive and mutually exclusive, and checked for errors.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is a master sheet?
answer_html:
• A master sheet is a large data sheet on which the coded data of all subjects are entered, with each row representing one subject and each column one variable or item (demographic variables, item responses, total scores).
  • It may be prepared on paper or in a spreadsheet (Excel) or statistical software.
  • It is the basis for tabulation and statistical analysis, allows easy checking of errors, and is usually attached in the appendix of the research report.
  • Every entry is cross-checked against the original tool before analysis.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is meant by interpretation of data?
answer_html:
• Interpretation is the process of explaining the meaning and significance of the results of analysis in relation to the study's objectives, hypotheses and theoretical framework.
  • It involves comparing the findings with earlier studies, explaining unexpected results, recognising limitations, and drawing conclusions and implications for nursing.
  • Good interpretation is objective and cautious – it does not claim more than the data show (for example, a correlation does not prove causation).
  • It forms the basis of the discussion chapter and of the recommendations made for practice, education and further research.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: (a) Define statistics and explain its uses in nursing. (4 marks) (b) Explain the measures of central tendency – mean, median and mode – with the method of calculation for ungrouped and grouped data. (8 marks) (c) State their merits and demerits. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Position of mean, median and mode in symmetrical and skewed distributions
labels: Three curves – symmetrical (normal) curve with mean = median = mode at the centre; positively skewed curve (tail to the right) with mode < median < mean; negatively skewed curve (tail to the left) with mean < median < mode

answer_html:
(a) Definition and uses of statistics (4 marks)

Definition

  • Statistics is the science of collecting, organising, summarising, presenting, analysing and interpreting numerical data, and of drawing valid conclusions and decisions from them.
  • Biostatistics is the application of statistics to biological, medical and health sciences.
  • Descriptive statistics describe and summarise data (frequency, percentage, averages, dispersion); inferential statistics draw conclusions about a population from a sample (tests of significance, estimation).

Uses of statistics in nursing

  • Nursing research – planning sample size, analysing data, testing hypotheses and drawing valid conclusions.
  • Nursing practice – interpreting patient data (vital-sign trends, growth charts, laboratory values), evaluating outcomes of nursing interventions, evidence-based practice (reading and judging research reports).
  • Nursing administration – calculating bed occupancy, average length of stay, staffing needs, infection rates, budgeting and quality indicators.
  • Nursing education – analysing examination results, evaluating teaching programmes, item analysis of tests.
  • Community health – vital statistics, morbidity and mortality rates, programme evaluation and planning (HMIS, NFHS data).

(b) Measures of central tendency (8 marks)

A measure of central tendency (average) is a single value that represents the centre or typical value of a set of data. The three common measures are the mean, median and mode.

1. Arithmetic mean (x̄)

  • Definition – the sum of all observations divided by their number.
  • Ungrouped data – x̄ = Σx ÷ n.
  • Example – haemoglobin (g/dl) of 10 antenatal women: 9.6, 10.2, 11.0, 10.8, 9.8, 12.1, 10.2, 11.4, 10.2, 9.7.
    • Σx = 105.0; n = 10; mean = 105.0 ÷ 10 = 10.5 g/dl.
  • Grouped data – x̄ = Σfx ÷ N, where x is the mid-point of each class and f its frequency.

Worked example (grouped data) – marks of 50 nursing students:

Marks (class) Mid-point (x) Frequency (f) fx Cumulative frequency (cf)
30–40 35 5 175 5
40–50 45 8 360 13
50–60 55 15 825 28
60–70 65 12 780 40
70–80 75 10 750 50
Total N = 50 Σfx = 2,890
  • Mean = Σfx ÷ N = 2,890 ÷ 50 = 57.8 marks.
  • Assumed mean (step-deviation) method gives the same answer with smaller numbers: taking A = 55 and class width h = 10, d′ = (x – A) ÷ h = –2, –1, 0, 1, 2; Σfd′ = –10 – 8 + 0 + 12 + 20 = 14; mean = A + (Σfd′ ÷ N) × h = 55 + (14 ÷ 50) × 10 = 55 + 2.8 = 57.8.

2. Median

  • Definition – the middle value when observations are arranged in ascending or descending order; it divides the data into two equal halves.
  • Ungrouped data – arrange the values; if n is odd, median = value of the ((n + 1) ÷ 2)th item; if n is even, the average of the two middle values.
    • Example – arranged Hb values: 9.6, 9.7, 9.8, 10.2, 10.2, 10.2, 10.8, 11.0, 11.4, 12.1; n = 10 (even), so median = (5th + 6th) ÷ 2 = (10.2 + 10.2) ÷ 2 = 10.2 g/dl.
  • Grouped data – Median = L + [(N/2 – cf) ÷ f] × h, where L = lower limit of the median class, cf = cumulative frequency of the class before it, f = frequency of the median class, h = class width.
    • Example (marks table) – N/2 = 25; the median class is 50–60 (cumulative frequency first exceeds 25); L = 50, cf = 13, f = 15, h = 10.
    • Median = 50 + [(25 – 13) ÷ 15] × 10 = 50 + 8 = 58 marks.

3. Mode

  • Definition – the value that occurs most frequently in the data.
  • Ungrouped data – the value with the highest frequency; in the Hb example 10.2 g/dl occurs three times, so mode = 10.2 g/dl. Data may be unimodal, bimodal or have no mode.
  • Grouped data – Mode = L + [(f₁ – f₀) ÷ (2f₁ – f₀ – f₂)] × h, where L = lower limit of the modal class (the class with the highest frequency), f₁ = its frequency, f₀ = frequency of the class before, f₂ = frequency of the class after.
    • Example – modal class 50–60; L = 50, f₁ = 15, f₀ = 8, f₂ = 12, h = 10.
    • Mode = 50 + [(15 – 8) ÷ (30 – 8 – 12)] × 10 = 50 + (7 ÷ 10) × 10 = 57 marks.
  • Empirical relationship (moderately skewed data) – Mode ≈ 3 Median – 2 Mean.

(c) Merits and demerits (3 marks)

Measure Merits Demerits Best used for
Mean Uses every observation; rigidly defined; easy to calculate; suitable for further statistical work (SD, t-test) Affected by extreme values; cannot be used for open-ended classes or qualitative data Interval and ratio data that are roughly symmetrical (Hb, weight, BP)
Median Not affected by extreme values; can be found for open-ended classes and ordinal data; easy to understand Does not use all observations; less suitable for algebraic treatment Skewed data (income, length of hospital stay), ordinal data
Mode Simple; not affected by extremes; can be used for nominal (qualitative) data; shows the most typical value May not exist or may be more than one; unstable in small samples; not suitable for further calculations Nominal data (most common blood group, commonest complaint)

In a symmetrical distribution the mean, median and mode are equal; in skewed distributions they separate.

(d) Choosing the appropriate average – examples

  • Mean – average birth weight of babies in a ward, mean knowledge score before and after teaching, mean BP of a group – where data are roughly symmetrical.
  • Median – length of hospital stay (a few patients stay for months and would pull the mean up), family income, time to first breastfeed – where data are skewed or contain extreme values.
  • Mode – the commonest blood group, the most frequent complaint in an OPD, the most common type of delivery – where data are categorical.
  • When reporting skewed data, give the median with the interquartile range rather than the mean with SD.

(e) Other averages (brief)

  • Weighted mean – each value is multiplied by its weight (importance or frequency) before averaging; used, for example, to combine marks of subjects with different credits.
  • Geometric mean – the nth root of the product of n values; used for rates of growth and for data such as antibody titres that increase in multiples.
  • Harmonic mean – the reciprocal of the mean of reciprocals; used for averaging rates such as speed.

(f) Important properties of the arithmetic mean

  • The sum of deviations of all observations from the mean is zero (for the BP data in the next answer, Σ(x – x̄) = 0).
  • The sum of squared deviations is smallest when taken from the mean – the basis of the standard deviation.
  • The combined mean of two groups = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂) ÷ (n₁ + n₂); for example, 20 students with mean 60 and 30 students with mean 50 give a combined mean of (1,200 + 1,500) ÷ 50 = 54.

Nursing importance

  • Nurses use averages every day – average patient census, mean pain score, median length of stay – and must choose the right average for the type of data to avoid misleading conclusions.

Conclusion Statistics is an essential tool for nursing research and practice. The mean, median and mode summarise data by a single typical value; the choice among them depends on the type and distribution of the data.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: (a) Define dispersion and list the measures of dispersion. (3 marks) (b) Explain the range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation, with the calculation of standard deviation for a given set of data. (8 marks) (c) Explain the coefficient of variation and the uses of standard deviation. (4 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and measures of dispersion (3 marks)

Definition

  • Dispersion (variability) is the extent to which the individual observations are spread or scattered around the central value (average).
  • Two groups can have the same mean but very different spread; for example, two wards may have the same average patient age (50 years) but one has patients aged 45–55 and the other 15–85. An average alone is therefore incomplete.

Measures of dispersion

  • Absolute measures (in the same units as the data) – range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, standard deviation and variance.
  • Relative measure (without units) – coefficient of variation, used to compare variability of different variables.

(b) Range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation (8 marks)

Example data – systolic BP (mm Hg) of 8 women attending an ANC clinic: 110, 120, 116, 124, 130, 118, 122, 112. Arranged in order: 110, 112, 116, 118, 120, 122, 124, 130; mean = 952 ÷ 8 = 119 mm Hg.

1. Range

  • Range = highest value – lowest value.
  • Example – 130 – 110 = 20 mm Hg.
  • Merits – simplest, quick (used in quality control, daily temperature charts). Demerits – depends only on two extreme values; affected by outliers; ignores the rest of the data.

2. Quartile deviation (semi-interquartile range)

  • Quartiles divide ordered data into four equal parts; Q₁ (first quartile) has 25% of values below it and Q₃ has 75% below it.
  • Interquartile range = Q₃ – Q₁; Quartile deviation = (Q₃ – Q₁) ÷ 2.
  • Example – Q₁ is at the (n + 1) ÷ 4 = 2.25th position = 112 + 0.25 × (116 – 112) = 113; Q₃ is at the 6.75th position = 122 + 0.75 × (124 – 122) = 123.5; QD = (123.5 – 113) ÷ 2 = 5.25 mm Hg.
  • Merits – not affected by extreme values; useful for skewed data and open-ended classes. Demerit – ignores the lowest and highest 25% of values.

3. Mean deviation (average deviation)

  • MD = Σ|x – x̄| ÷ n – the average of the absolute deviations from the mean (signs ignored).
  • Example – absolute deviations: 9, 1, 3, 5, 11, 1, 3, 7; Σ = 40; MD = 40 ÷ 8 = 5 mm Hg.
  • Merit – uses all values. Demerit – ignoring signs makes it unsuitable for further mathematical treatment.

4. Standard deviation (SD, σ or s)

  • Definition – the square root of the mean of the squared deviations of the observations from their mean (Karl Pearson). It is the most widely used and most reliable measure of dispersion.
  • Formulae – population SD: σ = √[Σ(x – x̄)² ÷ n]; sample SD (used in research): s = √[Σ(x – x̄)² ÷ (n – 1)]. The square of SD is the variance.

Calculation of SD for the BP data

BP (x) Deviation (x – x̄), x̄ = 119 (x – x̄)²
110 –9 81
120 1 1
116 –3 9
124 5 25
130 11 121
118 –1 1
122 3 9
112 –7 49
Σx = 952 Σ(x – x̄) = 0 Σ(x – x̄)² = 296
  • Sample SD = √(296 ÷ 7) = √42.29 ≈ 6.50 mm Hg.
  • (Population SD = √(296 ÷ 8) = √37 ≈ 6.08 mm Hg.)
  • Steps – (1) find the mean; (2) find each deviation from the mean; (3) square the deviations; (4) add the squares; (5) divide by n – 1 (or n); (6) take the square root.
  • For grouped data – SD = √[Σf(x – x̄)² ÷ N], using class mid-points.

Merits of SD – based on all observations; rigidly defined; least affected by sampling fluctuations; suitable for further statistical analysis. Demerits – somewhat difficult to calculate by hand; gives more weight to extreme values.

(c) Coefficient of variation and uses of SD (4 marks)

Coefficient of variation (CV)

  • CV = (SD ÷ Mean) × 100 – a relative measure of dispersion expressed as a percentage.
  • Example – CV = (6.50 ÷ 119) × 100 ≈ 5.5%.
  • Uses – to compare the variability of two or more series with different units or very different means (for example, variability of birth weight in grams versus length in centimetres); the series with the higher CV is more variable (less consistent).

Uses of standard deviation

  • Describes the spread of data along with the mean (reported as mean ± SD, for example 119 ± 6.5 mm Hg).
  • In a normal distribution, mean ± 1 SD includes about 68%, ± 2 SD about 95% and ± 3 SD about 99.7% of observations – used to set normal ranges of laboratory values and growth charts.
  • Used to calculate the standard error, z-scores, confidence intervals and tests of significance (t-test).
  • Helps judge whether an individual value is unusual and compare consistency of groups.

(d) Variance and standard error

  • Variance is the square of the standard deviation (s² = 296 ÷ 7 ≈ 42.3 for the BP example); it is used in many statistical tests (for example ANOVA) but is expressed in squared units, so the SD is preferred for description.
  • Standard error of the mean (SE) = SD ÷ √n; for the BP example, SE = 6.50 ÷ √8 ≈ 2.30 mm Hg. The SD describes the spread of individual values, whereas the SE describes the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean; the SE becomes smaller as the sample size increases.

(e) Example of comparing variability with the coefficient of variation

  • In a newborn unit the mean birth weight is 2,800 g with SD 420 g (CV = 420 ÷ 2,800 × 100 = 15%), and the mean length is 49 cm with SD 2 cm (CV = 2 ÷ 49 × 100 ≈ 4.1%).
  • Although the units are different, the CV shows that birth weight is far more variable than length in this group.

(f) Interpreting dispersion in research reports

  • Results are usually written as mean ± SD (for example, post-test knowledge 14.1 ± 1.2); a small SD means the group performed uniformly, a large SD means wide individual differences.
  • When two groups have similar means but very different SDs, the intervention may have helped some subjects a great deal and others very little, which deserves discussion.
  • For skewed data the interquartile range with the median is more informative than the SD.

(g) Where each measure is useful in practice

  • Range – quick description of daily variation, such as the highest and lowest temperature or blood sugar of a patient in 24 hours, and the range of ages in a sample.
  • Quartile deviation / interquartile range – for skewed data such as length of stay, waiting time in OPD or income, reported with the median.
  • Standard deviation – for symmetrical measurements such as BP, Hb, birth weight and test scores, reported with the mean, and used in tests of significance.
  • Coefficient of variation – for comparing consistency, for example of two laboratories measuring Hb, or of students' performance in two subjects.

Nursing importance

  • Reporting the SD with the mean shows how consistent results are; nurses use these ideas in interpreting growth (z-scores in WHO growth charts), laboratory reference ranges and research findings.

Conclusion Measures of dispersion complete the picture given by averages. The standard deviation, calculated from the squared deviations about the mean, is the most useful measure, while the coefficient of variation compares variability across different series.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: (a) Explain inferential statistics and the steps of testing a hypothesis. (5 marks) (b) Explain the level of significance, p value, type I and type II errors, one-tailed and two-tailed tests and degrees of freedom. (6 marks) (c) Differentiate between parametric and non-parametric tests and explain how to choose an appropriate test. (4 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Inferential statistics and the steps of testing a hypothesis (5 marks)

Inferential statistics

  • Inferential statistics are methods that allow the researcher to draw conclusions (inferences) about a population from data obtained from a sample, and to judge whether observed differences or relationships are real or due to chance (sampling error).
  • Two main uses – estimation of population parameters (with confidence intervals) and hypothesis testing (tests of significance).

Steps of testing a hypothesis

  1. State the null hypothesis (H₀) – no difference or no relationship (for example, "there is no significant difference between the mean pre-test and post-test knowledge scores") – and the alternative/research hypothesis (H₁).
  2. Choose the level of significance (α) – usually 0.05 (5%), sometimes 0.01.
  3. Select the appropriate statistical test – based on the type of data, number of groups, whether samples are paired or independent, and the distribution (for example, paired t-test for pre- and post-test scores of the same group).
  4. Calculate the test statistic (t, χ², r, etc.) from the sample data.
  5. Determine the degrees of freedom and find the critical (table) value for the chosen α, or obtain the p value from software.
  6. Make a decision – if the calculated value is greater than the table value (or p < α), reject H₀ – the result is statistically significant; otherwise do not reject H₀.
  7. Interpret the result in the context of the study – for example, "the structured teaching programme was effective in improving knowledge (t = 7.10, df = 7, p <0.05)".

(b) Key concepts in hypothesis testing (6 marks)

1. Level of significance (α)

  • The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true that the researcher is willing to accept; conventionally 0.05 (a 5% risk), or 0.01 for stricter conclusions.
  • Confidence level = 1 – α (95% or 99%).

2. p value

  • The probability of obtaining a result as extreme as (or more than) the one observed, if the null hypothesis were true.
  • p < 0.05 → statistically significant – the difference is unlikely to be due to chance; p ≥ 0.05 → not significant.
  • Statistical significance is not the same as clinical importance; a tiny difference can be significant in a very large sample.

3. Type I and type II errors

Decision H₀ is actually true H₀ is actually false
Reject H₀ Type I error (α error) – a "false positive": concluding an intervention works when it does not Correct decision (power)
Do not reject H₀ Correct decision Type II error (β error) – a "false negative": missing a real effect
  • The probability of a type I error is α; the probability of a type II error is β.
  • Power of a test = 1 – β – the probability of detecting a real effect; increased by a larger sample size, larger effect and less variability.
  • Reducing α (for example, from 0.05 to 0.01) reduces type I error but increases type II error, unless the sample size is increased.

4. One-tailed and two-tailed tests

  • Two-tailed test – used with a non-directional hypothesis ("there is a difference"); the rejection region is divided between both ends of the distribution (2.5% each at α = 0.05).
  • One-tailed test – used with a directional hypothesis ("post-test score will be higher"); the whole rejection region lies in one tail; it is more powerful but must be justified before the analysis.

5. Degrees of freedom (df)

  • The number of values in a calculation that are free to vary after certain restrictions are applied; needed to read critical values from statistical tables.
  • Examples – paired t-test: df = n – 1; independent t-test: df = n₁ + n₂ – 2; chi-square: df = (rows – 1) × (columns – 1).

6. Confidence interval – a range of values within which the population parameter is expected to lie with a stated confidence (for example, 95% CI of the mean = mean ± 1.96 × standard error).

(c) Parametric and non-parametric tests, and choosing a test (4 marks)

Point Parametric tests Non-parametric (distribution-free) tests
Assumptions Data normally distributed, interval or ratio level, homogeneity of variance, adequate sample Few assumptions; no need for normal distribution
Level of data Interval / ratio Nominal or ordinal (or skewed interval data)
Power More powerful when assumptions are met Less powerful
Examples t-test (independent, paired), ANOVA, Pearson's r, z-test Chi-square, Mann–Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal–Wallis, Spearman's rank correlation, sign test

Choosing an appropriate test

Research situation Parametric test Non-parametric alternative
Compare means of two independent groups Independent (unpaired) t-test Mann–Whitney U test
Compare pre- and post-test of the same group Paired t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Compare three or more groups One-way ANOVA Kruskal–Wallis test
Association between two categorical variables – Chi-square test (Fisher's exact test for small numbers)
Relationship between two variables Pearson's correlation Spearman's rank correlation

(d) Statistical significance and clinical significance

  • A result is statistically significant when it is unlikely to be due to chance (p <0.05); it is clinically significant when the difference is large enough to matter to patients or practice.
  • In a very large sample, a reduction of pain score by 0.2 points may be statistically significant but clinically useless; in a small sample, an important improvement may fail to reach significance because of low power.
  • Researchers should therefore report the size of the effect (mean difference, confidence interval) along with the p value.

(e) Common mistakes in hypothesis testing

  • Choosing the test after seeing the data, or changing from a two-tailed to a one-tailed test to obtain significance.
  • Applying parametric tests to clearly skewed or ordinal data, or the chi-square test to percentages or small expected frequencies.
  • Performing many tests on the same data without adjustment, which increases false-positive findings.
  • Saying that a hypothesis is "proved", or interpreting "not significant" as "no difference at all".

(f) Reporting results

  • Results are reported with the name of the test, the calculated value, degrees of freedom and p value – for example, "χ² = 7.5, df = 1, p <0.05" or "paired t = 7.10, df = 7, p <0.001" – and statistical software provides exact p values.

(g) Example of interpretation

  • "The mean post-test knowledge score (14.1) was significantly higher than the pre-test score (11.1); paired t = 7.10, df = 7, p <0.05. Hence H₀ is rejected and the structured teaching programme is considered effective in improving knowledge."

Nursing importance

  • Understanding significance, p values and errors helps nurses read research critically – to judge whether a reported "significant effect" is believable and important enough to change practice.

Conclusion Inferential statistics allow generalisation from samples to populations. Testing a hypothesis requires a clear null hypothesis, a chosen level of significance, the correct parametric or non-parametric test and careful interpretation that considers errors, power and clinical importance.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the scales (levels) of measurement, with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Measurement is the assignment of numbers to objects or events according to rules. S. S. Stevens described four scales (levels) of measurement; the level of a variable decides which statistics and tests can be used.

1. Nominal scale

  • The lowest level; numbers or names are used only to classify into categories with no order or quantity.
  • Examples – sex (male = 1, female = 2), blood group, religion, marital status, diagnosis, yes/no responses.
  • Permissible statistics – frequency, percentage, mode, chi-square test.

2. Ordinal scale

  • Categories are ranked in order, but the intervals between ranks are not equal or known.
  • Examples – grades of pain (mild, moderate, severe), stages of cancer, socio-economic class, levels of knowledge (adequate, moderate, inadequate), Likert responses, ranks in an examination.
  • Permissible statistics – frequency, percentage, median, percentiles, Spearman's rank correlation, Mann–Whitney and other non-parametric tests.

3. Interval scale

  • Ordered categories with equal intervals between values, but no true (absolute) zero; ratios are not meaningful.
  • Examples – temperature in °C or °F (0 °C does not mean "no temperature"; 40 °C is not "twice as hot" as 20 °C), IQ scores, calendar years.
  • Permissible statistics – mean, SD, Pearson correlation, t-test, ANOVA.

4. Ratio scale

  • The highest level – equal intervals and a true zero, so ratios are meaningful.
  • Examples – height, weight, age, pulse rate, blood pressure, haemoglobin, income, number of children, length of hospital stay (a weight of 60 kg is twice 30 kg).
  • Permissible statistics – all statistics, including the coefficient of variation and geometric mean.

Summary

Scale Categories Order Equal intervals True zero Example
Nominal ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ Blood group
Ordinal ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ Pain grade
Interval ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ Temperature in °C
Ratio ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Body weight

Why the level matters – calculating a mean of religion codes or of blood groups is meaningless, and a mean of ordinal pain grades can mislead; nominal data are analysed with frequencies and chi-square, ordinal data with medians and rank tests, and interval or ratio data with means, SD and parametric tests. A ratio variable can be converted to a lower level (for example, age in years grouped into age categories), but not the reverse.

Conclusion Identifying whether a variable is nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio is the first step in choosing the correct average, measure of dispersion and test of significance.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the construction of a frequency distribution, with an example.
answer_html:
Introduction Raw data collected in research are usually a large, unorganised mass of numbers. A frequency distribution is a table that shows how often each value or group of values (class) occurs, which condenses the data and shows its pattern.

1. Terms

  • Class interval – a group of values (for example, 9.0–9.9 g/dl); class width (h) – the difference between the limits (here 1 g/dl).
  • Class limits (lower and upper); class boundaries – the true limits midway between adjoining classes (for example, 8.95–9.95), used in graphs.
  • Exclusive method (10–20, 20–30; upper limit excluded) and inclusive method (10–19, 20–29).
  • Frequency (f) – number of observations in a class; relative frequency (f ÷ N) or percentage; cumulative frequency (cf) – running total.

2. Steps of construction

  1. Find the range (highest – lowest value).
  2. Decide the number of classes (usually 5–15; Sturges' rule k = 1 + 3.322 log N may guide).
  3. Calculate the class width ≈ range ÷ number of classes, rounded to a convenient figure.
  4. Write the class intervals so that every observation fits into one class (no overlaps or gaps).
  5. Tally each observation into its class (groups of five: ||||).
  6. Count the frequencies; add percentage and cumulative frequency columns; check that the total equals N.
  7. Give the table a number and title.

3. Example – haemoglobin (g/dl) of 30 antenatal women: 8.2, 9.5, 10.1, 11.3, 9.8, 10.6, 12.0, 8.9, 10.4, 11.1, 9.2, 10.8, 11.6, 10.0, 9.6, 12.4, 10.3, 8.5, 11.0, 10.7, 9.9, 11.8, 10.5, 9.4, 7.8, 10.9, 11.4, 10.2, 9.1, 12.6.

  • Range = 12.6 – 7.8 = 4.8; six classes of width 1 g/dl are convenient.
Hb (g/dl) Tally Frequency (f) Percentage Cumulative frequency
7.0–7.9 | 1 3.3 1
8.0–8.9 ||| 3 10.0 4
9.0–9.9 |||| || 7 23.3 11
10.0–10.9 |||| |||| 10 33.3 21
11.0–11.9 |||| | 6 20.0 27
12.0–12.9 ||| 3 10.0 30
Total 30 100
  • The table shows at once that the largest group (one-third) has Hb of 10–10.9 g/dl, and that 11 women (36.7%) have Hb below 10 g/dl.

4. Uses – condenses data; shows the shape of the distribution; basis for graphs (histogram, frequency polygon, ogive) and for calculating the mean, median, mode and SD of grouped data.

Conclusion A frequency distribution, constructed with suitable class intervals, tally marks, frequencies and cumulative frequencies, turns raw data into a meaningful summary for analysis and graphical presentation.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the graphical presentation of a frequency distribution – histogram, frequency polygon, frequency curve and ogive.

diagram.caption: Histogram with frequency polygon and less-than ogive of the haemoglobin distribution of 30 women
labels: Left – histogram of six adjoining bars on class boundaries 7–8
and a frequency polygon joining the mid-points of the bar tops
closed at the base; right – less-than ogive plotting cumulative frequencies 1
with the median read at cf = 15

answer_html:
Introduction Graphs present the frequency distribution of quantitative (continuous) data in a visual form that shows the shape, centre and spread of the distribution at a glance. (Bar diagrams and pie charts are used for qualitative/discrete data.)

General rules – a clear title and number; x-axis (horizontal) for the variable and y-axis (vertical) for frequency; suitable, labelled scales beginning at zero for frequency; neat, simple and not overcrowded; the source noted.

1. Histogram

  • A set of adjacent (touching) rectangles, one for each class interval; the width of each bar equals the class width (plotted on class boundaries) and the height equals the frequency (with equal class widths).
  • There are no gaps between the bars because the data are continuous.
  • Example – the Hb distribution (7–8, 8–9 … 12–13 g/dl with frequencies 1, 3, 7, 10, 6, 3) gives six touching bars, the tallest over 10–11 g/dl.
  • Use – shows the shape (symmetrical, skewed) and the modal class; mode can be estimated graphically.

2. Frequency polygon

  • Formed by plotting the frequencies against the mid-points of the classes and joining the points with straight lines; the polygon is closed by joining to the mid-points of an empty class at each end on the base line.
  • It can be drawn over a histogram (joining the mid-points of the tops of the bars) or on its own.
  • Use – comparing two or more distributions on the same graph (for example, Hb of rural and urban women).

3. Frequency curve

  • A smooth free-hand curve drawn through the points of a frequency polygon; shows the general shape – normal (bell-shaped), skewed, bimodal.

4. Ogive (cumulative frequency curve)

  • A graph of cumulative frequencies plotted against class boundaries.
  • "Less than" ogive – cumulative frequencies (1, 4, 11, 21, 27, 30) plotted against upper boundaries (8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13); it rises from left to right.
  • "More than" ogive – plotted against lower boundaries; it falls from left to right.
  • Use – to find the median, quartiles and percentiles graphically: draw a horizontal line from N/2 (15) on the y-axis to the curve and drop a perpendicular to the x-axis to read the median (about 10.4 g/dl here); the two ogives intersect at the median.

Conclusion Histograms, frequency polygons, frequency curves and ogives show the pattern of continuous data clearly; the ogive also gives the median and other positional values graphically.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the salient features of the normal distribution (normal probability curve) and its importance.

diagram.caption: Normal probability curve with areas under the curve
labels: Symmetrical bell-shaped curve with the mean
median and mode at the centre; vertical lines at ±1
±2 and ±3 SD marked with the areas 68.27%
95.45% and 99.73%; tails approaching but never touching the base line; points of inflection at ±1 SD

answer_html:
Introduction The normal distribution (normal probability curve or Gaussian curve) is the most important theoretical distribution in statistics. Many biological measurements – height, weight, blood pressure, haemoglobin, birth weight, intelligence scores – are approximately normally distributed in large populations, and many statistical tests assume normality.

Salient features

  1. Bell-shaped – the curve rises to a single peak in the middle and falls off gradually on both sides.
  2. Perfectly symmetrical about the mean – the left half is a mirror image of the right half.
  3. Mean = median = mode – all three lie at the centre (peak) of the curve.
  4. Asymptotic – the two tails approach the base line but never touch it, extending theoretically to infinity.
  5. Total area under the curve = 1 (100%), with 50% on each side of the mean.
  6. Fixed proportions of area between multiples of the SD (the 68–95–99.7 rule):
    • mean ± 1 SD covers about 68.27% of observations;
    • mean ± 2 SD about 95.45% (± 1.96 SD exactly 95%);
    • mean ± 3 SD about 99.73%.
  7. Defined completely by two parameters – the mean (location) and the standard deviation (spread); a larger SD gives a flatter, wider curve.
  8. Points of inflection (where the curve changes direction) lie at mean ± 1 SD.
  9. Skewness is zero and the curve is mesokurtic (moderate peakedness).
  10. Unimodal – it has only one peak.
  11. The standard normal curve has mean 0 and SD 1; any value can be converted to a z-score: z = (x – mean) ÷ SD.

Importance

  • Basis of parametric tests (t-test, z-test, ANOVA) and of confidence intervals.
  • Used to set normal reference ranges (mean ± 2 SD) for laboratory values and to interpret growth charts (z-scores below –2 SD indicate underweight, stunting or wasting).
  • Helps identify unusual (abnormal) values and outliers.
  • The sampling distribution of means approaches normality in large samples (central limit theorem).

Deviations from normality – skewness (positive – tail to the right, mean > median > mode; negative – tail to the left) and abnormal kurtosis (leptokurtic – too peaked; platykurtic – too flat).

Conclusion The normal curve is symmetrical, bell-shaped and defined by its mean and SD, with known areas under it; these properties make it the foundation of statistical inference and of normal ranges used daily in health care.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain correlation – Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation and Spearman's rank correlation – with examples.

diagram.caption: Scatter diagrams showing types of correlation
labels: Five small scatter plots – perfect positive (points on a rising straight line
high positive (points close to a rising line)
high negative (points close to a falling line)

answer_html:
Introduction Correlation is a statistical method that measures the degree and direction of the relationship between two quantitative variables (for example, BMI and blood pressure, or study hours and marks). The coefficient of correlation (r) ranges from –1 to +1.

1. Types

  • Positive correlation – both variables increase or decrease together (height and weight).
  • Negative correlation – one increases as the other decreases (age and physical activity; Hb and fatigue score).
  • Zero correlation – no relationship.
  • Perfect correlation – r = +1 or –1 (all points on a straight line); rare in biology.
  • Interpretation of strength (common guide) – 0 to ±0.3 weak, ±0.3 to ±0.7 moderate, ±0.7 to ±1 strong.
  • A scatter diagram (plotting pairs of values) gives a quick visual idea of the relationship.

2. Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation (product-moment correlation)

  • For interval/ratio data with a linear relationship:
  • r = Σ(x – x̄)(y – ȳ) ÷ √[Σ(x – x̄)² × Σ(y – ȳ)²].
  • Example – number of antenatal education sessions attended (x) and knowledge score (y) of 5 mothers:
x y x – x̄ (x̄ = 3) y – ȳ (ȳ = 26) (x – x̄)(y – ȳ) (x – x̄)² (y – ȳ)²
1 10 –2 –16 32 4 256
2 20 –1 –6 6 1 36
3 25 0 –1 0 0 1
4 35 1 9 9 1 81
5 40 2 14 28 4 196
Total 75 10 570
  • r = 75 ÷ √(10 × 570) = 75 ÷ 75.5 ≈ +0.99 – a very strong positive correlation: mothers who attended more sessions had higher knowledge scores.

3. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (ρ)

  • Used for ordinal (ranked) data or when data are not normally distributed:
  • ρ = 1 – [6Σd² ÷ n(n² – 1)], where d = difference between the two ranks of each subject.
  • Example – two examiners rank 6 students in a practical examination: Examiner A – 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Examiner B – 2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5.
    • d = –1, 1, –1, 1, –1, 1; Σd² = 6; n = 6.
    • ρ = 1 – (6 × 6) ÷ (6 × 35) = 1 – 36 ÷ 210 = 1 – 0.171 ≈ +0.83 – strong agreement between the examiners.

4. Important points

  • Correlation does not prove causation – two variables may both be affected by a third factor.
  • r² (coefficient of determination) shows the proportion of variation in one variable explained by the other.
  • The significance of r is tested to see whether the relationship could be due to chance.
  • Uses in nursing research – relating knowledge and practice, stress and coping, BMI and BP, and establishing test–retest reliability of tools.

Conclusion Pearson's r measures linear relationship between quantitative variables and Spearman's ρ between ranked variables; both range from –1 to +1 and must be interpreted with care, remembering that correlation is not causation.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the chi-square test – its uses, conditions and steps, with an example.
answer_html:
Introduction The chi-square (χ²) test, introduced by Karl Pearson, is a non-parametric test of significance for categorical (nominal or ordinal) data. It compares the observed frequencies with the frequencies expected if the null hypothesis were true.

1. Uses

  • Test of association (independence) – whether two attributes are associated (for example, association between knowledge level and education – the most common use in nursing student projects).
  • Test of goodness of fit – whether observed data fit a theoretical distribution or expected ratio.
  • Test of homogeneity – whether different groups have the same distribution.

2. Formula – χ² = Σ[(O – E)² ÷ E], where O = observed frequency and E = (row total × column total) ÷ grand total.

  • For a 2 × 2 table with cells a, b, c, d: χ² = N(ad – bc)² ÷ [(a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d)].

3. Conditions

  • Data are frequencies (counts), not percentages or means; categories are mutually exclusive.
  • Observations are independent; the sample is random (preferably) and reasonably large.
  • Expected frequency in each cell should be 5 or more; otherwise apply Yates' correction (2 × 2 tables) or use Fisher's exact test, or combine categories.

4. Steps

  1. State H₀ – there is no association between the two variables.
  2. Set the level of significance (0.05).
  3. Prepare the contingency table of observed frequencies and calculate the expected frequencies.
  4. Calculate χ² using the formula.
  5. Find degrees of freedom = (rows – 1)(columns – 1).
  6. Compare with the table value; if the calculated χ² is greater, reject H₀ – the association is significant.

5. Worked example – exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) at 6 weeks among 80 mothers, with and without antenatal breastfeeding education:

Group EBF – yes EBF – no Total
Received education 30 (a) 10 (b) 40
No education 18 (c) 22 (d) 40
Total 48 32 N = 80
  • Expected frequencies – (40 × 48) ÷ 80 = 24 for the "yes" cells and (40 × 32) ÷ 80 = 16 for the "no" cells.
  • χ² = (30 – 24)²/24 + (10 – 16)²/16 + (18 – 24)²/24 + (22 – 16)²/16 = 1.5 + 2.25 + 1.5 + 2.25 = 7.5.
  • (Check with the 2 × 2 formula: 80 × (30 × 22 – 10 × 18)² ÷ (40 × 40 × 48 × 32) = 80 × 480² ÷ 24,57,600 = 7.5.)
  • df = (2 – 1)(2 – 1) = 1; table value at 0.05 = 3.84.
  • Since 7.5 > 3.84, H₀ is rejected – there is a significant association between antenatal breastfeeding education and exclusive breastfeeding (p <0.05).

Conclusion The chi-square test is a simple and widely used test for association between categorical variables; correct calculation of expected frequencies, attention to its conditions and comparison with the table value lead to valid conclusions.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain Student's t-test – its types, assumptions and steps, with an example of the paired t-test.
answer_html:
Introduction The t-test, developed by William Gosset (who wrote under the pen-name "Student"), is a parametric test used to compare means, especially when the sample is small (traditionally less than 30) and the population SD is unknown. It is the most common test in nursing studies evaluating the effectiveness of an intervention.

1. Types

  • One-sample t-test – compares a sample mean with a known or hypothesised population value.
  • Independent (unpaired) samples t-test – compares the means of two separate groups (for example, experimental and control groups); df = n₁ + n₂ – 2.
  • Paired (dependent) t-test – compares two measurements on the same subjects (pre-test and post-test, before and after an intervention); df = n – 1.

2. Assumptions

  • Data are on an interval or ratio scale and approximately normally distributed.
  • Observations are independent (between subjects); groups have similar variances (independent t-test).
  • Samples are randomly selected (ideally).
  • If these are not met, non-parametric alternatives (Mann–Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank) are used.

3. Formula for the paired t-test – t = d̄ ÷ (s_d ÷ √n), where d = difference between paired scores, d̄ = mean difference, s_d = SD of the differences, n = number of pairs.

4. Worked example – knowledge scores of 8 student nurses before and after a structured teaching programme on biomedical waste:

Student Pre-test Post-test d (post – pre) d – d̄ (d – d̄)²
1 10 14 4 1 1
2 12 15 3 0 0
3 9 13 4 1 1
4 14 16 2 –1 1
5 11 15 4 1 1
6 13 15 2 –1 1
7 8 12 4 1 1
8 12 13 1 –2 4
Mean 11.125 14.125 Σd = 24; d̄ = 3 Σ = 10
  • s_d = √[Σ(d – d̄)² ÷ (n – 1)] = √(10 ÷ 7) = √1.43 ≈ 1.195.
  • Standard error = s_d ÷ √n = 1.195 ÷ 2.828 ≈ 0.423.
  • t = 3 ÷ 0.423 ≈ 7.10; df = 8 – 1 = 7; table value at 0.05 (two-tailed) = 2.365.
  • Since 7.10 > 2.365, H₀ is rejected – the mean post-test score is significantly higher than the pre-test score; the teaching programme was effective (p <0.05).

5. Steps (summary) – state H₀ and H₁ → choose α → check assumptions → calculate the means, differences, SD and standard error → compute t → find df and the critical value → decide and interpret.

Conclusion The t-test compares means of two sets of scores; the paired t-test is the standard way to test the effectiveness of an intervention in pre-test post-test studies, provided its assumptions are satisfied.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Define statistics.
tags: analysis and interpretation of numerical data
answer_html:
• Statistics is the science of collecting, organising, summarising, presenting, analysing and interpreting numerical data in order to draw valid conclusions and make decisions under uncertainty.
  • In the plural sense, "statistics" also means numerical facts themselves (for example, vital statistics).
  • Its application to biology, medicine and health is called biostatistics; it is divided into descriptive and inferential statistics.
  • In nursing it is used to analyse research data, interpret patient and community health data, and evaluate services and teaching programmes.
  • Example – calculating the average length of stay in a ward or the percentage of anaemic antenatal women in a block.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Differentiate between descriptive and inferential statistics.
answer_html:
Descriptive statistics Inferential statistics
Describe and summarise the data of the sample Draw conclusions about the population from the sample
Frequency, percentage, mean, median, mode, SD, tables and graphs Tests of significance (t-test, chi-square, ANOVA), correlation significance, confidence intervals
No generalisation beyond the data Generalisation with a known probability of error
Example – "mean knowledge score was 14.1 ± 1.2" Example – "the gain in knowledge was significant (t = 7.10, p <0.05)"

Most research reports use both – descriptive statistics first, then inferential statistics to test the hypotheses.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Differentiate between a parameter and a statistic.
answer_html:
Parameter Statistic
A numerical characteristic of the population A numerical characteristic of the sample
Usually fixed but unknown Known (calculated), varies from sample to sample
Denoted by Greek letters – μ (mean), σ (SD), ρ (correlation) Denoted by Roman letters – x̄ (mean), s (SD), r (correlation)
Example – the true mean Hb of all pregnant women in a district Example – the mean Hb of 100 women sampled from that district

The statistic is used to estimate the parameter; the difference between them is the sampling error.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is skewness?
tags: mean greater than median greater than mode
answer_html:
• Skewness is the lack of symmetry in a frequency distribution – the tail extends more on one side.
  • Positive (right) skew – the long tail is on the right; mean > median > mode (for example, length of hospital stay, income).
  • Negative (left) skew – the long tail is on the left; mean < median < mode (for example, age at death in a developed population, scores in an easy test).
  • In a symmetrical distribution, skewness is zero and mean = median = mode.
  • In skewed data the median is a better average than the mean.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is kurtosis?
answer_html:
• Kurtosis is the degree of peakedness (or flatness) of a frequency curve compared with the normal curve.
  • Mesokurtic – moderately peaked, like the normal curve (coefficient of kurtosis about 3).
  • Leptokurtic – more peaked than normal, with values concentrated around the mean.
  • Platykurtic – flatter than normal, with values widely spread.
  • Together with skewness, it describes the shape of a distribution and helps judge whether data are approximately normal.
  • Example – the scores of a very easy test, where most students score close to the average, give a leptokurtic curve.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What are quartiles and percentiles?
answer_html:
• Quartiles are the three values (Q₁, Q₂, Q₃) that divide ordered data into four equal parts; Q₁ has 25% of observations below it, Q₂ is the median (50%), and Q₃ has 75% below it.
  • Percentiles divide the data into 100 equal parts; the Pth percentile is the value below which P% of observations fall (the 50th percentile = median).
  • Uses – the interquartile range (Q₃ – Q₁) as a measure of spread; growth charts (a child's weight at the 3rd or 97th percentile), ranking of students and reference ranges.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What are degrees of freedom?
tags: number of values free to vary
independent t-test n1 plus n2 minus 2
chi-square rows minus 1 times columns minus 1
answer_html:
• Degrees of freedom (df) are the number of observations in a calculation that are free to vary after certain restrictions (such as a fixed mean or fixed totals) have been applied.
  • They are needed to read the critical value of a test from statistical tables.
  • Examples – paired t-test: df = n – 1; independent t-test: df = n₁ + n₂ – 2; chi-square: df = (rows – 1) × (columns – 1) – for a 2 × 2 table, df = 1.
  • Simple illustration – if the mean of 5 numbers is fixed, only 4 can be chosen freely; the fifth is then decided, so df = 4.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is a confidence interval?
answer_html:
• A confidence interval (CI) is a range of values, calculated from sample data, within which the true population value (parameter) is expected to lie with a stated level of confidence – usually 95%.
  • For a mean, 95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × standard error.
  • A narrow CI indicates a precise estimate (usually from a large sample); a wide CI indicates uncertainty.
  • Example – "mean systolic BP 119 mm Hg (95% CI 114–124)"; CIs are reported alongside p values because they show the size and precision of an effect.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: (a) Define a research report and state its purposes. (3 marks) (b) Describe the format (contents) of a research report (dissertation) of a nursing study. (8 marks) (c) Explain the qualities of a good research report. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Format (contents) of a nursing research report
labels: Three stacked blocks – Preliminary pages (title page
figures and appendices); Main body (Chapter I Introduction

answer_html:
Introduction Research is complete only when its findings are communicated. A study that stays in the investigator's file adds nothing to nursing knowledge or practice. The research report is the main written means by which a study is shared, evaluated and put to use.

(a) Definition and purposes

  • A research report is a written, systematic and complete account of a research study – the problem, the methods used, the findings and the conclusions – presented in a prescribed format so that others can understand, evaluate, use and, if needed, repeat the study.
  • When it is prepared for an academic degree it is called a dissertation (usually at master's level) or a thesis (usually at doctoral level); B.Sc. Nursing students prepare a project report of their group study.

Purposes

  1. To communicate the findings to nurses, other professionals, administrators and the public.
  2. To add to the body of nursing knowledge and provide a basis for evidence-based practice.
  3. To serve as a permanent record of the study that can be consulted later.
  4. To allow others to evaluate (critique) and replicate the study.
  5. To fulfil the requirement of a degree or the accountability to a funding agency.
  6. To suggest implications and recommendations for practice, education, administration and further research.

Types of research reports (brief) – thesis or dissertation; journal article; project report to a funding agency; conference paper and poster; abstract; research brief (a short summary for administrators and policy-makers); popular articles and press notes for the public.

(b) Format (contents) of a research report The exact format is prescribed by each university or institution, but most nursing dissertations have three parts.

I. Preliminary pages

  • Title page – the full title (for example, "A study to assess the effectiveness of a structured teaching programme on knowledge regarding kangaroo mother care among postnatal mothers in selected hospitals"), the names of the investigator(s) and guide, the degree, institution, university and year.
  • Certificates – from the guide and the head of the institution, and the approval of the institutional ethics committee where required; a declaration by the investigator that the work is original.
  • Acknowledgement – thanks to the guide, participants, institution and others who helped.
  • Abstract – a brief summary (commonly 200–300 words) of the problem, objectives, methods, main findings and conclusion, followed by keywords.
  • Table of contents, list of tables, list of figures (graphs and diagrams), list of appendices and list of abbreviations.

II. Main body (five chapters)

  • Chapter I – Introduction
    • background of the study and the need (significance) for the study, supported by statistics;
    • statement of the problem and objectives;
    • operational definitions of key terms;
    • hypotheses, assumptions and delimitations;
    • conceptual framework (placed in Chapter II in some formats) and an outline of the rest of the report.
  • Chapter II – Review of literature
    • studies and other literature related to the problem, organised under sub-headings (for example, literature on KMC and neonatal outcomes, on mothers' knowledge of KMC, and on the effectiveness of teaching programmes);
    • the conceptual or theoretical framework, such as a general systems model or a nursing theory.
  • Chapter III – Research methodology
    • research approach and design (with a schematic diagram of the design);
    • variables, setting, population, sample, sample size and sampling technique, inclusion and exclusion criteria;
    • development and description of the tool, its validity and reliability;
    • pilot study, ethical considerations (permission, informed consent, confidentiality) and the procedure of data collection;
    • plan for data analysis.
  • Chapter IV – Analysis and interpretation of data
    • data organised in sections according to the objectives (for example, Section A – demographic variables; Section B – pre-test knowledge; Section C – effectiveness of the programme; Section D – association of knowledge with demographic variables);
    • presented in tables and graphs with their interpretation and the results of tests of hypotheses.
  • Chapter V – Discussion, summary, conclusion, implications and recommendations
    • discussion – the findings compared and contrasted with those of earlier studies;
    • summary of the whole study and its major findings;
    • conclusion drawn from the findings;
    • implications for nursing practice, nursing education, nursing administration and nursing research;
    • limitations of the study;
    • recommendations for further studies (for example, a similar study on a larger sample, or a comparative study between rural and urban mothers).

III. Supplementary (reference) pages

  • References (bibliography) in the prescribed style (for example, APA or Vancouver), listing every source cited in the text.
  • Appendices – letters of permission, ethics committee approval, informed consent form, the tool in English and the regional language, content-validity certificates and the list of experts, blueprint and answer key, the teaching programme or intervention protocol, the master data sheet and the certificate of language editing.

(c) Qualities of a good research report

  1. Accuracy and honesty – data, calculations and quotations are correct; findings are reported as they are, including negative or unexpected results; nothing is fabricated, altered or plagiarised.
  2. Clarity and simplicity – clear, simple, grammatically correct language; technical terms defined; short sentences and paragraphs.
  3. Logical organisation – follows the prescribed format, moving logically from the problem to the conclusion, with suitable headings and sub-headings.
  4. Objectivity – impersonal and unbiased presentation, usually in the third person ("the investigator found" rather than "I found") unless the style guide allows otherwise; conclusions based only on the data.
  5. Completeness with conciseness – includes everything needed to understand, evaluate and replicate the study, without repetition or unnecessary detail.
  6. Correct tense – past tense for what was done and found (methods and results); present tense for established facts and for conclusions; a proposal, by contrast, is written in the future tense.
  7. Consistency – the same terms, abbreviations, units and numbering throughout; tables and figures numbered, titled and referred to in the text.
  8. Proper documentation – every source cited in the text and listed in the references in one style; permission obtained for using copyrighted tools.
  9. Good presentation – typed to the institution's specifications (font, spacing, margins, page numbering), proof-read and properly bound.
  10. Suited to the audience – full technical detail for academic readers; a simple summary (research brief) for administrators, policy-makers or the public.

Common errors to avoid – copying literature without citation; objectives that do not match the analysis; tables given without interpretation; different sample sizes in different chapters; conclusions that go beyond the data; and the tool or consent form missing from the appendices.

Steps in writing the report (brief) – plan and outline the chapters → write the first draft → revise and edit → review by the guide → final typing, proof-reading and binding → submission.

Nursing importance

  • A well-written report allows nurse administrators and clinicians to judge whether findings can be applied in their own wards and communities.
  • Student reports kept in the college library and shared through digital repositories help later batches identify gaps and avoid duplication.
  • Writing a report develops the scientific thinking, organisation and writing skills needed for publication and evidence-based practice.
  • Honest reporting protects patients and the profession from the harm caused by misleading findings.

Conclusion A research report is the written record of a study, organised into preliminary pages, five main chapters and supplementary pages. Accuracy, clarity, objectivity and the correct format make it credible and useful, and turn a completed study into knowledge that can improve nursing care.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the methods of communicating (disseminating) research findings, with emphasis on oral and poster presentation.

diagram.caption: Layout of a research poster
labels: authors and institution across the top; three columns below – introduction and objectives; methods (design
procedure); results with two graphs and a table; a final box of conclusion and implications

answer_html:
Introduction Dissemination is the communication of research findings to the people who can use them – nurses, other health professionals, administrators, policy-makers, participants and the public. The method is chosen according to the audience and the purpose.

1. Written methods

  • Thesis, dissertation or project report submitted to the institution or university.
  • Journal articles in peer-reviewed nursing and health journals – the most permanent and widely accessible method.
  • Research brief or executive summary for administrators and policy-makers – one or two pages in simple language with the key recommendations.
  • Newsletters, college magazines, books and chapters, and institutional or national digital repositories.

2. Oral (paper) presentation

  • Given at conferences, seminars, CNE programmes, ward meetings and journal clubs; usually 10–15 minutes followed by questions.
  • Content – title, background and need, objectives, methods, key results, conclusion and implications; only the most important findings, not the whole thesis.
  • Slides – about one slide per minute; few words per slide, large font, simple graphs instead of big tables, and a consistent design.
  • Delivery – rehearse within the time limit; speak to the audience rather than reading the slides; anticipate questions and answer honestly.

3. Poster presentation

  • A visual summary of a study displayed on a board at a conference; the presenter stands beside the poster to discuss it with viewers.
  • Sections – title, authors and institution; introduction; objectives; methods; results (graphs, tables); conclusion and implications; a few key references; acknowledgement; contact details or a QR code.
