  • Design principles – size and orientation as specified by the organisers; a title readable from a distance; brief text in bullet points (about 500–800 words in all); a logical flow from left to right and top to bottom; graphs and pictures rather than dense text; consistent, contrasting colours; enough white space; no spelling errors.
  • Advantages – allows one-to-one discussion and networking; suits beginners and student researchers; findings can be seen at a glance.

4. Electronic and other methods

  • Institutional websites, e-posters, webinars, professional social-media groups and podcasts.
  • Mass media (newspapers, radio, local television) for findings of public interest, written in simple language.
  • Feedback to participants and the community – sharing results with the hospital, village or school where the study was done, for example through a meeting with mothers and ASHAs.

Guidelines for effective dissemination – identify the target audience; present findings accurately without exaggeration; protect the confidentiality of participants; acknowledge funding and contributors; obtain the institution's permission where required; and disseminate negative findings as well.

Conclusion Findings reach practice only when they are communicated. Written reports and articles provide a permanent record, while oral and poster presentations allow direct discussion; together they help bridge the gap between research and practice.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain the critique (critical appraisal) of a research article – its purposes, principles and guidelines.
answer_html:
Introduction A research critique (critical appraisal) is an objective, systematic and balanced evaluation of a research report that identifies its strengths and weaknesses in order to judge the validity of its findings and their usefulness for practice. It is not merely fault-finding.

Purposes

  • To decide whether the findings are trustworthy and can be applied in practice (evidence-based practice).
  • To develop the critical thinking of students and nurses, for example in journal clubs.
  • To identify gaps for future research and to improve one's own research and writing.
  • To review manuscripts for journals (peer review) and proposals for research or ethics committees.

Principles

  • Read the whole article, more than once, before judging it.
  • Be objective, balanced and specific – point out strengths as well as weaknesses, with reasons.
  • Judge the study against accepted research standards while considering the limitations of its setting; criticise the work, not the researcher.
  • Offer constructive suggestions.

Guidelines – questions to ask about each part

  1. Title – is it clear and concise, and does it indicate the variables and population?
  2. Abstract – does it summarise the problem, methods, results and conclusion?
  3. Problem and purpose – is the problem clearly stated, significant to nursing and researchable? Are the objectives and hypotheses clear and testable?
  4. Review of literature – is it relevant, recent, critically analysed and drawn mainly from primary sources? Is a framework described?
  5. Methodology – is the design appropriate to the objectives? Are the setting, population, sample size and sampling technique described and adequate? Are inclusion and exclusion criteria stated? Is the tool described, with its validity and reliability? Was a pilot study done? Were ethical approval and informed consent obtained?
  6. Data analysis and results – are the statistical tests appropriate to the level of data and the design? Are tables and figures clear and consistent with the text? Are all objectives and hypotheses answered?
  7. Discussion and conclusion – are the findings compared with other studies? Are the conclusions supported by the data, and are the limitations acknowledged?
  8. Implications and recommendations – are they realistic and relevant to practice?
  9. References – are they accurate, complete and in one style?
  10. Overall judgement – is the study credible, and can it be applied in my setting?

Tools that help – structured checklists such as the CASP and JBI critical appraisal checklists, and reporting guidelines such as CONSORT (randomised trials), STROBE (observational studies) and COREQ (qualitative research).

Conclusion A systematic critique tells the nurse how far a study can be trusted and used; it builds the habit of reading research critically, which is the foundation of evidence-based nursing.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Explain research utilisation in nursing – its meaning, types, models and the barriers to using research findings.
answer_html:
Introduction Research utilisation is the use of the findings of a study, or a group of studies, in a practical application – in patient care, education or administration – that is separate from the original research. It aims to close the research–practice gap, the long delay between the discovery of new knowledge and its use in daily care.

Research utilisation and EBP – research utilisation starts from the research (what can be done with these findings?), whereas evidence-based practice starts from a clinical problem and combines the best research evidence with clinical expertise and patient preferences; research utilisation is a part of the wider EBP movement.

Types of utilisation

  • Instrumental (direct) – findings are used directly to change practice, for example adopting a new protocol for preventing pressure injuries.
  • Conceptual – findings change the way nurses think about a problem, even if practice does not change immediately.
  • Persuasive (symbolic) – findings are used to persuade administrators or policy-makers to support a change.

Models of research utilisation (outline)

  1. CURN project (Conduct and Utilization of Research in Nursing, USA) – a pioneering project that helped nurses identify research-based innovations, judge their fit, implement them on a trial basis and evaluate the results.
  2. Stetler model – guides an individual nurse through the phases of preparation (purpose and context), validation (critique of the studies), comparative evaluation and decision-making (fit, feasibility, current practice), translation and application, and evaluation.
  3. Iowa model – an organisational model that begins with triggers – problem-focused (for example, a rise in catheter-associated urinary tract infections) or knowledge-focused (a new guideline or study) – then asks whether the topic is a priority, forms a team, gathers and critiques the evidence, pilots the change if the evidence is sufficient, evaluates it, adopts it in practice and disseminates the results.

Barriers to research utilisation (commonly grouped as in Funk's BARRIERS scale)

  • Nurse (adopter) – lack of knowledge of research and statistics, lack of skill in critique, unawareness of findings, resistance to change, lack of confidence.
  • Organisation (setting) – lack of time and staff, lack of authority to change procedures, poor administrative support, poor access to journals and the internet.
  • Research (quality) – conflicting or poor-quality studies, findings not replicated or not applicable to the local setting.
  • Presentation (communication) – reports full of technical language and statistics, and findings not readily available or not in a usable form.

Strategies to promote utilisation

  • Teaching research and critique in nursing programmes; journal clubs and CNE.
  • Administrative support – time, library and internet access, research committees, mentors and nurse researchers in hospitals.
  • Presenting findings in simple language – research briefs, posters, protocols and guidelines.
  • Collaboration between nursing colleges and hospitals; pilot projects; and recognition of nurses who implement change.

Conclusion Research utilisation turns findings into better care. Understanding its types, following a structured model and tackling barriers at the level of the nurse, the organisation, the research and its communication help bring proven practices to the bedside.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is a research proposal? Explain its purposes and contents.
answer_html:
Introduction A research proposal (also called a synopsis or research protocol) is a written plan of a proposed study that describes what the investigator intends to study, why, and how it will be done. It is prepared and approved before data collection begins.

Purposes

  • To obtain approval from the guide, the research committee and the university, and clearance from the institutional ethics committee.
  • To apply for funding or a grant.
  • To serve as a blueprint for the investigator during the study and to help foresee problems.
  • To act as an agreement between the investigator, the guide or institution and any funding agency.
  • To show that the investigator has the knowledge and ability to carry out the study.

Contents (common format)

  1. Title – clear and specific, indicating the variables, population and setting.
  2. Introduction – background and need for the study, with statistics.
  3. Statement of the problem, objectives, hypotheses, operational definitions, assumptions and delimitations.
  4. Conceptual framework, where applicable.
  5. Brief review of literature – key related studies showing what is known and the gap to be filled.
  6. Methodology – research approach and design, variables, setting, population, sample size (with its calculation) and sampling technique, inclusion and exclusion criteria, the tool and its validity and reliability, the plan for a pilot study, the data collection procedure and the plan for data analysis (the statistical tests to be used).
  7. Ethical considerations – permission from authorities, ethics committee approval, informed consent, confidentiality and the right to withdraw.
  8. Work plan (timeline) – often shown as a Gantt chart of activities against months.
  9. Budget – personnel, materials, printing, travel and data analysis (for funded studies).
  10. References and appendices – the draft tool, consent form and letters seeking permission.

Qualities of a good proposal

  • Clear, concise and logically organised, following the prescribed format and length.
  • Written in the future tense ("the investigator will…").
  • Objectives, design, tool and analysis consistent with one another.
  • Feasible within the time, money and resources available.
  • Ethical and properly referenced.

Difference from the report – the proposal describes what will be done and is written before the study; the report describes what was done and found and is written after it.

Conclusion A carefully written proposal is the foundation of a successful study: it secures approval and funding, protects participants and keeps the investigator on track.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is an impact factor?
answer_html:
• The journal impact factor (JIF) measures how often the average article in a journal is cited in a particular year; it is published annually by Clarivate in the Journal Citation Reports.
  • Impact factor for 2025 = citations received in 2025 by items published in 2023 and 2024 ÷ number of citable items published in 2023 and 2024.
  • Example – 300 citations to 150 articles gives an impact factor of 2.0.
  • It reflects the influence of a journal, not the quality of an individual article or author; related measures include the h-index (for authors) and CiteScore (Scopus).

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What is peer review?
answer_html:
• Peer review is the evaluation of a manuscript (or a research proposal) by independent experts in the same field before it is accepted for publication or funding.
  • It checks originality, scientific validity, ethics and clarity, and helps the editor decide to accept, ask for minor or major revision, or reject it.
  • Types – single-blind (reviewers know the authors), double-blind (neither knows the other) and open peer review (identities disclosed).
  • Articles in peer-reviewed journals are therefore considered more reliable evidence than unreviewed publications.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: What are DOI and ORCID iD?
answer_html:
• DOI (Digital Object Identifier) – a unique, permanent identifier assigned to a digital document such as a journal article. It begins with "10." and a prefix identifying the publisher, followed by a suffix identifying the item; added after https://doi.org/ it always opens the article even if the web address changes. APA style includes the DOI in references.
  • ORCID iD (Open Researcher and Contributor ID) – a free, unique 16-digit identifier for a researcher (written 0000-0000-0000-0000) that distinguishes authors with similar names and links all their publications.

subject: Nursing Research and Statistics
question: Differentiate between a research report (dissertation) and a research article.
answer_html:
Research report (dissertation) Research article
Lengthy, complete account of every step of the study Condensed – a few thousand words, within the journal's limit
Preliminary pages, five chapters and supplementary pages IMRAD format – introduction, methods, results and discussion
Tools, consent form and master sheet given in appendices Appendices usually omitted
Evaluated by the guide and university examiners Evaluated by the journal editor and peer reviewers
Read by a limited audience (examiners, library users) Reaches a wide professional audience
Purpose – degree requirement or report to a sponsor Purpose – wide dissemination of findings
